entries.meaning: To a small degree; slightly, or for a short time. ---
examples: I'm a bit worried about the weather.
Could you turn the music down a bit?
Let's wait a bit before we call him.
entries.position: before its word — or end, after a verb (rest a bit)
entries.contrast: Before a plain adjective it prefers unwelcome qualities: a bit late, a bit tired, not a bit wonderful — use a little or pretty there. Before a noun it needs of: a bit of luck.

entries.meaning: With voices only, without instruments. ---
examples: The choir sang the last hymn a cappella.
When the sound system failed, she finished the song a cappella.
The group records all its music a cappella.
entries.contrast: Also an adjective before a noun (an a cappella group). Spelled with two p's and two l's.

entries.meaning: A good deal has 2 distinct senses.
examples: She looks a good deal better than she did last week.
The new route is a good deal shorter.
He travels a good deal for work.
We've talked about it a good deal at home.

senses.head: Much; considerably, with a comparative or too
examples: She looks a good deal better than she did last week.
The new route is a good deal shorter.

senses.head: A lot; much or often, with a verb
examples: He travels a good deal for work.
We've talked about it a good deal at home.

entries.position: before its word — before a comparative (a good deal better); end after a verb
entries.contrast: Not the noun a good deal (выгодная сделка): I got a good deal on the car. Before a noun it needs of: a good deal of time.

entries.meaning: A great deal has 2 distinct senses.
examples: Things are a great deal easier now.
The repair cost a great deal more than we expected.
She has traveled a great deal since she retired.
I've thought about your offer a great deal.

senses.head: Much; far, with a comparative or too
examples: Things are a great deal easier now.
The repair cost a great deal more than we expected.

senses.head: Very much or very often, with a verb
examples: She has traveled a great deal since she retired.
I've thought about your offer a great deal.

entries.position: before its word — before a comparative (a great deal easier); end after a verb
entries.contrast: More formal than a lot, and the natural choice in affirmative sentences where much sounds stiff: He worries a great deal, not He worries much.

entries.meaning: Ordered or priced item by item, not as part of a set meal or package. ---
examples: We skipped the buffet and ordered a la carte.
Side dishes are sold a la carte.
The app lets you buy extra features a la carte.
entries.modifies: verbs of ordering, buying and pricing
entries.form: French à la carte, 'by the menu'; usually written without the accent in American English
entries.contrast: Also an adjective (an a la carte menu). It has spread from restaurants to anything sold item by item.

entries.meaning: To a small degree; slightly. ---
examples: I'm a little tired after the flight.
Could you speak a little louder?
Let's rest a little before we go on.
entries.position: before its word — or end, after a verb (relax a little)
entries.contrast: A little is positive (немного); little without a is negative (мало): He sleeps a little in the afternoon vs He sleeps little. Unlike a bit, it sits comfortably before pleasant adjectives: a little happier.

entries.meaning: A lot has 2 distinct senses.
examples: I feel a lot better today.
This phone is a lot cheaper online.
We go to the beach a lot in the summer.
Thanks a lot for your help.
He talks a lot when he's nervous.

senses.head: Much; far, with a comparative
examples: I feel a lot better today.
This phone is a lot cheaper online.

senses.head: Very much or very often, with a verb
examples: We go to the beach a lot in the summer.
Thanks a lot for your help.
He talks a lot when he's nervous.

entries.position: end — after the verb and object; before its word with a comparative (a lot better)
entries.contrast: Always two words: alot is a misspelling. It cannot go before a plain adjective: a lot better, but not a lot good — say very good. Informal; in formal writing prefer much or a great deal.

entries.meaning: Slightly; a little. ---
examples: She seemed a trifle annoyed by the question.
The soup was a trifle too salty.
He arrived a trifle late, as usual.
entries.contrast: Mostly written; in speech Americans say a little or a bit. The noun trifle means a small unimportant thing.

entries.meaning: Surprised and briefly thrown off balance, in be taken aback. ---
examples: I was taken aback by how rude he was.
She seemed a little taken aback when I mentioned the price.
We were all taken aback by the news.
entries.type: manner — only in the fixed phrase taken aback
entries.modifies: the passive be taken in be taken aback

entries.meaning: Abjectly has 2 distinct senses.
examples: He apologized abjectly for the mistake.
She begged abjectly for one more chance.
The plan failed abjectly.
Many families there live in abjectly poor conditions.

senses.head: In a humble, ashamed way
examples: He apologized abjectly for the mistake.
She begged abjectly for one more chance.

senses.head: Completely and hopelessly, of failure or poverty
examples: The plan failed abjectly.
Many families there live in abjectly poor conditions.

entries.position: end — or before its word (abjectly poor)
entries.modifies: verbs of apologizing and failing; adjectives like poor

entries.meaning: With skill; competently. ---
examples: The team was ably led by a young captain.
She handled the reporters' questions ably.
He was ably assisted by two graduate students.
entries.position: end — or mid, before a participle (ably assisted)

entries.meaning: In a way that is not normal or usual. ---
examples: Her blood pressure was abnormally high.
It's been an abnormally warm winter.
The cells were growing abnormally.
entries.position: before its word — before adjectives (abnormally high); end with verbs

entries.meaning: Very badly, in a shocking or offensive way. ---
examples: The workers were treated abominably by the new owners.
He behaved abominably at his sister's wedding.
The hotel staff were abominably rude to us.
entries.position: end — or before its word (abominably rude)
entries.modifies: verbs of behaving and treating; adjectives

entries.meaning: About has 2 distinct senses.
examples: The drive takes about three hours.
There were about fifty people at the party.
I'll be there at about six.
I'm about ready to leave.
We're just about done with the kitchen.
He's about the only person who knows the password.

senses.head: Approximately; a little more or less than
examples: The drive takes about three hours.
There were about fifty people at the party.
I'll be there at about six.

senses.head: Almost; nearly, often in just about
examples: I'm about ready to leave.
We're just about done with the kitchen.
He's about the only person who knows the password.

entries.position: before its word — before numbers and amounts, and before ready, done, finished
entries.modifies: numbers, amounts and times; adjectives like ready and done
entries.contrast: Before a noun, about is usually a preposition meaning 'о, про' (a book about dogs), and be about to means 'вот-вот, собираться'. For 'here and there' Americans say around (walk around) where British English says walk about.

entries.meaning: Most importantly; more than anything else. ---
examples: Above all, don't panic.
She wanted, above all, to be taken seriously.
Be kind, be honest, and above all, be yourself.
entries.type: focusing — marks the most important item
entries.position: front or end — often front with a comma, or right before the item it stresses
entries.modifies: a whole clause, or the phrase it singles out
entries.contrast: Not first of all: first of all orders points (во-первых), above all ranks them (самое главное).

entries.meaning: Abreast has 2 distinct senses.
examples: The path was too narrow to walk two abreast.
Three police cars drove abreast down the highway.
I read the news every morning to keep abreast of what's happening.
Doctors have to stay abreast of new research.

senses.head: Side by side, facing the same way
examples: The path was too narrow to walk two abreast.
Three police cars drove abreast down the highway.

senses.head: Up to date with news or developments, in keep abreast of or stay abreast of
examples: I read the news every morning to keep abreast of what's happening.
Doctors have to stay abreast of new research.

entries.русский: в ряд, бок о бок; в курсе
entries.type: place; also manner in keep abreast of
entries.modifies: verbs of moving and standing; keep and stay + of

entries.meaning: Suddenly and unexpectedly; also in a short, curt way. ---
examples: The car stopped abruptly.
The meeting ended abruptly when the fire alarm went off.
“I have to go,” she said abruptly, and hung up.
entries.position: end — or mid, before the verb
entries.modifies: verbs, especially stop, end, leave, turn

entries.meaning: Without paying attention to what you are doing. ---
examples: He nodded absently, still looking at his phone.
She absently stirred her coffee.
“Sure, sure,” he said absently.
entries.position: end — or mid, before the verb

entries.meaning: Forgetfully, because your mind is on something else. ---
examples: I absentmindedly left my keys in the fridge.
She was absentmindedly twisting her ring.
He walked out absentmindedly without paying.

entries.meaning: In terms of general ideas rather than real examples. ---
examples: It's hard for young children to think abstractly.
He talked abstractly about justice but never gave an example.
The problem gets easier once you stop thinking about it so abstractly.

entries.meaning: To a ridiculous degree; in a ridiculous way. ---
examples: Rent in this city is absurdly high.
The instructions were absurdly complicated.
He was dressed absurdly for a funeral.
entries.position: before its word — before adjectives (absurdly expensive); end with verbs

entries.meaning: Abundantly has 2 distinct senses.
examples: She made it abundantly clear that she wasn't interested.
It's abundantly obvious that the plan won't work.
Wildflowers grow abundantly in these hills.
The region is abundantly supplied with fresh water.

senses.head: Very; completely, mostly in abundantly clear
examples: She made it abundantly clear that she wasn't interested.
It's abundantly obvious that the plan won't work.

senses.head: In large amounts; plentifully
examples: Wildflowers grow abundantly in these hills.
The region is abundantly supplied with fresh water.

entries.position: before its word — mostly in abundantly clear; end in the 'plentifully' sense
entries.modifies: adjectives like clear and obvious; verbs of growing and supplying

entries.meaning: In an insulting or cruel way. ---
examples: The fan was thrown out for shouting abusively at the referee.
Neighbors said he had treated the dog abusively for years.
She reported a customer who spoke to her abusively.

entries.meaning: Extremely badly; to a terrible degree. ---
examples: The team played abysmally in the second half.
Pay for teachers there is abysmally low.
The service was abysmally slow.
entries.position: before its word — before adjectives; end with verbs (played abysmally)

entries.meaning: In terms of school, studies or scholarship. ---
examples: Our son is doing well academically but struggles to make friends.
The school admits only academically gifted students.
Academically, it was her best year.
entries.type: viewpoint — 'as far as studies are concerned'
entries.position: before its word — before adjectives (academically gifted); end with verbs; front with a comma
entries.modifies: adjectives, participles, verbs, and whole sentences

entries.meaning: Well enough to be accepted; satisfactorily. ---
examples: The car ran acceptably after the repair.
Is the water acceptably clean?
Students must perform acceptably on the final exam to pass.
entries.position: end — or before its word (acceptably safe)

entries.meaning: By mistake; without meaning to. ---
examples: I accidentally deleted the whole file.
She accidentally locked herself out of the car.
The fire was started accidentally by a cigarette.
entries.position: mid — before the main verb; also end
entries.form: -ly from accidental — spelled -ally, often said ak-suh-DENT-lee
entries.contrast: Accidentally means 'by mistake, without meaning to'. In questions, Russian случайно ('do you happen to…') is by any chance (Do you have a pen, by any chance?), never accidentally.

entries.meaning: Correctly and exactly, without mistakes. ---
examples: The forecast accurately predicted the storm.
Please fill out the form accurately.
We can't measure the distance more accurately without a laser.
entries.position: end — or mid, before the verb

entries.meaning: In a way that shows you think someone did something wrong. ---
examples: She looked at me accusingly.
“You ate the last cookie,” he said accusingly.
The dog stared accusingly at its empty bowl.

entries.meaning: Acoustically has 2 distinct senses.
examples: The new concert hall is acoustically excellent.
Acoustically, the room was a disaster.
The band played the last three songs acoustically.
She recorded the whole album acoustically in her kitchen.

senses.head: In terms of sound
examples: The new concert hall is acoustically excellent.
Acoustically, the room was a disaster.

senses.head: On instruments that are not electrically amplified
examples: The band played the last three songs acoustically.
She recorded the whole album acoustically in her kitchen.

entries.position: before its word — before adjectives (acoustically perfect); end in the 'unplugged' sense
entries.modifies: adjectives and verbs of playing and recording

entries.meaning: Equally for everyone or everything in a group; without exception. ---
examples: The company cut salaries across the board.
Prices rose across the board last month.
The new rules apply across the board.
entries.type: manner — applying equally to every member of a group
entries.modifies: verbs of cutting, raising and applying
entries.contrast: Also an adjective with hyphens before a noun: an across-the-board tax cut.

entries.meaning: In a busy, energetic way that involves doing things. ---
examples: We're actively looking for a new office.
She's been actively involved in the campaign from the start.
Try to take part more actively in class discussions.
entries.position: mid — before the main verb; also end

entries.meaning: Very strongly or sharply, of a feeling or a problem. ---
examples: I was acutely aware that everyone was watching me.
She felt the loss acutely.
The shortage of nurses is acutely felt in rural hospitals.
entries.position: before its word — before adjectives, especially aware and embarrassed; end with verbs like feel

entries.meaning: Forever; again and again without end. ---
examples: The list of complaints could go on ad infinitum.
We can't keep extending the deadline ad infinitum.
The pattern repeats ad infinitum.
entries.modifies: verbs of going on and repeating; the end of a list

entries.meaning: Repeated so often or so long that people are sick of it. ---
examples: The ad played ad nauseam during the game.
They discussed the budget ad nauseam.
He quotes that movie ad nauseam.
entries.type: frequency — so often that it becomes tiresome
entries.modifies: verbs of repeating, discussing and playing

entries.meaning: Firmly, refusing to change your mind. ---
examples: He adamantly denied taking the money.
The mayor is adamantly opposed to the new stadium.
She adamantly refused to apologize.
entries.position: mid — before the verb, especially refuse, deny, oppose
entries.modifies: verbs and participles of refusing and opposing

entries.meaning: Well enough for the purpose. ---
examples: Were you adequately prepared for the interview?
The house wasn't adequately heated.
He couldn't explain his decision adequately.
entries.position: end — or before its word (adequately prepared)

entries.meaning: In terms of management and official procedures. ---
examples: The two campuses are administratively separate.
The case was handled administratively, not in court.
Administratively, the merger was a nightmare.
entries.position: before its word — before adjectives; end with verbs; front with a comma

entries.meaning: Very well, in a way that deserves respect. ---
examples: She handled a difficult situation admirably.
The report is admirably clear.
The volunteers performed admirably under pressure.
entries.position: end — or before its word (admirably clear)
entries.form: -ly from admirable — stressed on AD, not on the -mire- of admire

entries.meaning: In a way that shows admiration. ---
examples: He looked at the painting admiringly.
People whistled admiringly as the old car drove past.
“You built all this yourself?” she asked admiringly.

entries.meaning: In a sweet, charming way. ---
examples: The puppy was adorably clumsy.
She looked adorably confused.
The kids were dressed adorably in matching sweaters.
entries.position: before its word — before adjectives (adorably clumsy); end with verbs

entries.meaning: With great love and admiration. ---
examples: The dog gazed adoringly at its owner.
She smiled adoringly at her new baby.
He talks adoringly about his grandkids.
entries.modifies: verbs of looking, smiling and speaking

entries.meaning: Floating without being steered or tied; figuratively, without direction or support. ---
examples: The boat was adrift for three days before it was found.
The fishermen were cast adrift when their engine failed.
Without a leader, the party has been left adrift.
entries.position: end — mostly after be, cast, set or leave
entries.modifies: verbs like be, float, cast, set and leave

entries.meaning: Skillfully and cleverly, especially in a tricky situation. ---
examples: She adroitly changed the subject.
The senator adroitly avoided answering the question.
He steered the car adroitly through the traffic.
entries.position: end — or mid, before the verb

entries.meaning: In a way that gives an advantage or benefit. ---
examples: The house is advantageously located near the train station.
She invested her savings advantageously.
The new rules could work advantageously for small businesses.
entries.position: end — or before a participle (advantageously located)

entries.meaning: In a harmful or negative way. ---
examples: The drought adversely affected this year's harvest.
Patients who reacted adversely to the drug were removed from the study.
Rising interest rates could adversely impact home sales.
entries.position: mid — before the verb, especially affect; also end
entries.modifies: verbs, especially affect, impact and react

entries.meaning: Deliberately, after careful thought, especially about a choice of words. ---
examples: I use the word “disaster” advisedly.
He chose his words advisedly.
The term “crisis” is used advisedly in this report.
entries.position: end — mostly in I use the word advisedly
entries.modifies: verbs of choosing and using words
entries.form: -ly from advised, with an extra syllable: uhd-VY-zid-lee

entries.meaning: In terms of beauty or appearance. ---
examples: The new bridge is both practical and aesthetically pleasing.
Aesthetically, I prefer the older design.
The furniture was chosen aesthetically, not for comfort.
entries.position: before its word — especially in aesthetically pleasing; front with a comma

entries.meaning: From or at a great distance. ---
examples: She had admired him from afar for years.
Visitors came from afar to see the festival.
From afar, the island looked deserted.
entries.type: place — formal, almost always in from afar
entries.modifies: verbs of seeing, coming and admiring

entries.meaning: In a friendly, easygoing way. ---
examples: He chatted affably with the other guests.
The host greeted us affably at the door.
She smiled affably and shook everyone's hand.
entries.modifies: verbs of talking, smiling and greeting

entries.meaning: In a loving, fond way. ---
examples: She hugged her grandson affectionately.
The old professor is affectionately known as “Doc.”
He patted the horse affectionately on the neck.
entries.position: end — or before a participle (affectionately known as)

entries.meaning: In a way that means yes. ---
examples: She nodded affirmatively.
Most of the people surveyed answered affirmatively.
If you can answer affirmatively to all three questions, you qualify.

entries.meaning: Far away from home or from the usual place or topic. ---
examples: Tourists now come from as far afield as Japan.
We had to look farther afield for a cheaper apartment.
The discussion wandered far afield from the original topic.
entries.type: place — mostly in far afield and farther afield
entries.modifies: verbs of traveling, looking and wandering

entries.meaning: Again, in a new way. ---
examples: After the fire, they had to start afresh.
Let's look at the problem afresh in the morning.
The committee decided to begin afresh with a new plan.
entries.type: manner — formal; in speech Americans usually say start over
entries.modifies: verbs like start, begin and look at

entries.meaning: Later; following something already mentioned. ---
examples: He left, and she arrived soon after.
I saw her the week before the wedding and the day after.
They got married and lived happily ever after.
entries.position: end — usually after a time word (soon after, the day after)
entries.modifies: verbs, with time words before it (soon, long, shortly, the week)
entries.contrast: With an object after is a preposition (after lunch); with a clause it is a conjunction (after we left). As an adverb it is most natural with a time word in front (soon after); on its own at the end of a sentence, careful writing prefers afterward or later.

entries.meaning: In a rough or imperfect way; to some extent. ---
examples: I speak Spanish, after a fashion.
The repair worked, after a fashion.
He apologized, after a fashion.
entries.type: degree — a downtoner: not well, but somewhat
entries.contrast: Nothing to do with fashion as clothing: She can sew, after a fashion means she sews, but not well.

entries.meaning: After all has 2 distinct senses.
examples: It didn't rain after all.
So you decided to come after all!
The test wasn't that hard after all.
Don't be so hard on him. After all, he's only six.
We should invite her; she is, after all, part of the team.

senses.head: In spite of what was expected or planned
examples: It didn't rain after all.
So you decided to come after all!
The test wasn't that hard after all.

senses.head: Used to give a reason that should be kept in mind
examples: Don't be so hard on him. After all, he's only six.
We should invite her; she is, after all, part of the team.

entries.position: front or end — end when it means despite what was expected, usually front when it gives a reason
entries.contrast: Not после всего, and not finally: for the last step in a sequence use finally or in the end. Position carries the meaning: He came after all (всё-таки пришёл) vs After all, he's your brother (он ведь твой брат).

entries.meaning: After the normal working or opening hours. ---
examples: The staff often stay after hours to finish orders.
The building is locked after hours.
I don't answer work email after hours.
entries.contrast: Also an adjective with a hyphen: an after-hours club.

entries.meaning: At a later time; after that. ---
examples: We went out for ice cream afterwards.
Afterwards, she couldn't remember what she'd said.
Shortly afterwards, the power went out.
entries.contrast: Americans usually say afterward, without the -s; afterwards is the British preference but is also common in the US.

entries.meaning: Many times; repeatedly. ---
examples: I've told you again and again to lock the door.
She watched the video again and again.
The same problem comes up again and again.
entries.русский: снова и снова, раз за разом

entries.meaning: As fast as possible, to finish before a deadline. ---
examples: Rescue teams are working against the clock to reach the miners.
We were racing against the clock to finish the report.
In the final round, contestants cook against the clock.
entries.type: manner — in a hurry to meet a deadline
entries.modifies: verbs like work, race and cook

entries.meaning: Aggressively has 2 distinct senses.
examples: The dog barked aggressively at the mail carrier.
He was pulled over for driving aggressively on the interstate.
The company is aggressively expanding into new markets.
The cancer was treated aggressively with surgery and chemotherapy.
We need to market the product more aggressively.

senses.head: In a hostile, threatening way
examples: The dog barked aggressively at the mail carrier.
He was pulled over for driving aggressively on the interstate.

senses.head: With great energy and determination to succeed
examples: The company is aggressively expanding into new markets.
The cancer was treated aggressively with surgery and chemotherapy.
We need to market the product more aggressively.

entries.position: end — or mid, before the verb

entries.meaning: To a painfully frustrating degree. ---
examples: The line moved agonizingly slowly.
They came agonizingly close to winning the title.
The wait for the test results was agonizingly long.
entries.position: before its word — before adjectives and adverbs, especially slow and close

entries.meaning: In a pleasant way. ---
examples: I was agreeably surprised by the food.
The evening passed agreeably with good wine and conversation.
The weather was agreeably mild for March.
entries.position: before its word — especially in agreeably surprised; end with verbs

entries.meaning: In a strong position, having prepared earlier than others or than needed. ---
examples: If you start saving now, you'll be ahead of the game.
She reads industry reports to stay ahead of the game.
We filed our taxes in February, so we're ahead of the game.
entries.type: manner — in a position of advantage

entries.meaning: Before the time something happens or is due; in advance. ---
examples: Call ahead of time to reserve a table.
I cook most of the meal ahead of time.
The train arrived ten minutes ahead of time.
entries.contrast: Everyday American for in advance. Compare on time (вовремя) and in time (успеть к сроку).

entries.meaning: Without a purpose or direction. ---
examples: We wandered aimlessly around the mall.
He spent the summer drifting aimlessly from job to job.
She was flipping aimlessly through the channels.
entries.modifies: verbs of moving and passing time

entries.meaning: In a light, careless way, as if something does not matter. ---
examples: “Oh, it's nothing,” she said airily.
He waved airily at the pile of bills.
The governor airily dismissed the report.
entries.position: end — or mid, before the verb

entries.meaning: With hands on the hips and elbows pointing out; of legs, spread out at odd angles. ---
examples: She stood in the doorway with arms akimbo.
The kids sprawled on the couch, legs akimbo.
He waited by the car, arms akimbo, looking annoyed.
entries.position: after its word — after arms, legs or elbows
entries.modifies: the nouns arms, legs and elbows in fixed phrases

entries.meaning: To a worrying degree; in a way that causes alarm. ---
examples: Crime rates have risen alarmingly in the past year.
The river was alarmingly high after the storm.
Alarmingly, nobody at the plant noticed the leak.
entries.position: before its word — before adjectives; end with verbs of change; front as a comment (Alarmingly, …)
entries.modifies: adjectives, verbs of change, and whole sentences

entries.meaning: Outdoors, especially of eating a meal. ---
examples: In summer we like to eat alfresco on the patio.
The restaurant lets you dine alfresco by the river.
Lunch was served alfresco under the trees.
entries.modifies: verbs like eat, dine and serve
entries.form: from Italian al fresco 'in the fresh air'; also written al fresco

entries.meaning: By using algebra. ---
examples: Solve the equation algebraically, then check your answer on a graph.
The rule can be expressed algebraically in one line.
Show algebraically that the two expressions are equal.
entries.modifies: verbs like solve, express and show

entries.meaning: The whole time; from the very beginning. ---
examples: I knew all along that he was lying.
The keys were in my pocket all along.
She was right all along.
entries.русский: всё это время, с самого начала
entries.contrast: With a following noun it is a preposition about space: trees all along the river. The adverb means the whole time, often with the sense that someone knew or was right: I knew it all along.

entries.meaning: All at once has 2 distinct senses.
examples: All at once, the lights went out.
All at once she started to cry.
Don't eat the candy all at once.
Everyone started talking all at once.

senses.head: Suddenly; without warning
examples: All at once, the lights went out.
All at once she started to cry.

senses.head: All together at the same time
examples: Don't eat the candy all at once.
Everyone started talking all at once.

entries.meaning: Considering everything; on the whole. ---
examples: All in all, it was a good year.
There were a few problems, but all in all the trip went well.
All in all, I'd recommend the hotel.
entries.русский: в общем и целом, в целом

entries.meaning: Suddenly and unexpectedly. ---
examples: All of a sudden, the dog started barking.
I felt dizzy all of a sudden.
Why are you so interested in cooking all of a sudden?
entries.contrast: More informal and more dramatic than suddenly. Many Americans say all of the sudden, but it is marked wrong in writing.

entries.meaning: All over has 2 distinct senses.
examples: I've looked all over for my glasses.
There was broken glass all over.
I ache all over after that workout.
She was shaking all over.

senses.head: Everywhere; in every part of a place
examples: I've looked all over for my glasses.
There was broken glass all over.

senses.head: Over the whole body or surface
examples: I ache all over after that workout.
She was shaking all over.

entries.contrast: With a following noun it is a preposition: all over the world. It's all over (всё кончено) is an adjective use meaning finished.

entries.meaning: All right has 2 distinct senses.
examples: The interview went all right, I think.
Are you getting along all right at the new job?
The old laptop still works all right.
That's him all right — I'd know that laugh anywhere.
She was angry all right.

senses.head: Well enough; satisfactorily
examples: The interview went all right, I think.
Are you getting along all right at the new job?
The old laptop still works all right.

senses.head: Certainly; without any doubt, after a statement
examples: That's him all right — I'd know that laugh anywhere.
She was angry all right.

entries.modifies: verbs; or a whole statement, placed after it
entries.contrast: Alright is common in informal writing but still marked wrong in formal American English. I'm all right (в порядке) and Is it all right if…? (можно ли) are adjective uses, and All right, let's go is an interjection.

entries.meaning: In spite of that; nevertheless. ---
examples: He's annoying, but I like him all the same.
All the same, you should have called.
I don't need a ride, but thanks all the same.
entries.position: front or end — front with a comma, or at the end of the clause
entries.contrast: It's all the same to me (мне всё равно) is a different, adjective use meaning it makes no difference.

entries.meaning: All the time has 2 distinct senses.
examples: She complains all the time.
This kind of thing happens all the time in big cities.
We eat at that diner all the time.
I searched everywhere, and the ticket was in my wallet all the time.
He was listening all the time we were talking.

senses.head: Very often; constantly
examples: She complains all the time.
This kind of thing happens all the time in big cities.
We eat at that diner all the time.

senses.head: During the whole of a period, often without someone knowing
examples: I searched everywhere, and the ticket was in my wallet all the time.
He was listening all the time we were talking.

entries.meaning: All the way has 2 distinct senses.
examples: We walked all the way home.
She drove all the way from Chicago.
Turn the volume all the way down.
I'm with you all the way.
Read the contract all the way through before you sign.

senses.head: For the whole distance
examples: We walked all the way home.
She drove all the way from Chicago.

senses.head: Completely; to the end
examples: Turn the volume all the way down.
I'm with you all the way.
Read the contract all the way through before you sign.

entries.modifies: verbs of movement; verbs of turning, reading and supporting

entries.meaning: As a group, in one place or at the same time. ---
examples: Let's sing it all together from the top.
Put the receipts all together in one folder.
It's nice to have the family all together for once.
entries.contrast: Not altogether (совсем; в целом): We sang all together vs I'm not altogether sure. Test: if you can split it — We all sang together — write two words.

entries.meaning: Counting everyone or everything; in all. ---
examples: All told, the repairs cost $4,000.
There were about fifty guests all told.
All told, we spent three weeks on the road.
entries.modifies: a whole clause, usually one with a number

entries.meaning: Much more than is good or wanted; far too. ---
examples: The vacation ended all too soon.
Mistakes like this are all too common.
I know that feeling all too well.
entries.type: degree — an intensifier with a regretful tone
entries.modifies: adjectives and adverbs (all too often, all too soon)

entries.meaning: High up in the air; upward. ---
examples: The winner held the trophy aloft.
Hot air keeps the balloon aloft.
The pilot stayed aloft for nine hours.
entries.modifies: verbs like hold, stay, keep and raise

entries.meaning: Next to someone or something, side by side. ---
examples: A police car pulled up alongside.
The boat came alongside, and a man threw us a rope.
She ran ahead, and her dog trotted alongside.
entries.form: along + side, written as one word
entries.contrast: With an object alongside is a preposition (parked alongside the curb, work alongside experts); without one it is an adverb.

entries.meaning: In a voice that other people can hear; not silently. ---
examples: The teacher asked me to read the poem aloud.
Sorry, I was just thinking aloud.
She laughed aloud at the joke.
entries.modifies: verbs of reading, thinking, laughing and wondering
entries.contrast: Aloud means 'so others can hear' (вслух), not 'in a loud voice' (громко, loudly): read aloud, but talk loudly. Out loud means the same as aloud and is more common in speech.

entries.meaning: In the order of the letters of the alphabet. ---
examples: The files are arranged alphabetically by last name.
List the countries alphabetically.
The books on this shelf are sorted alphabetically by author.

entries.meaning: Alright has 2 distinct senses.
examples: The interview went alright, I think.
Is the new printer working alright?
That's him alright — I'd know that laugh anywhere.
It's cold out there alright.

senses.head: Well enough; satisfactorily
examples: The interview went alright, I think.
Is the new printer working alright?

senses.head: Certainly; without any doubt, placed after the statement for emphasis
examples: That's him alright — I'd know that laugh anywhere.
It's cold out there alright.

entries.modifies: verbs; a whole statement in the 'certainly' sense
entries.form: an informal one-word spelling of all right
entries.contrast: Many teachers and editors still mark alright as wrong, so write all right in formal work. In Are you alright? it is an adjective, and in Alright, let's go it is a reply word — neither is the adverb.

entries.meaning: One after the other, again and again. ---
examples: The movie is alternately funny and sad.
She works alternately in Boston and New York.
Add the flour and the milk alternately, a little at a time.
entries.position: before its word — before adjectives (alternately funny and sad); end or mid with verbs
entries.modifies: pairs of adjectives or verbs, and verbs
entries.contrast: Alternately means 'taking turns, first one and then the other'; alternatively means 'as another option' (как вариант). Americans sometimes use alternately for 'as another option', but careful writers keep them apart.

entries.meaning: Altogether has 3 distinct senses.
examples: He stopped drinking altogether.
I'm not altogether sure she's right.
The idea was altogether new to me.
That comes to $45 altogether.
Altogether, about 200 people showed up.
The weather was bad, but altogether it was a good trip.
Altogether, I'd say the meeting went well.

senses.head: Completely; entirely
examples: He stopped drinking altogether.
I'm not altogether sure she's right.
The idea was altogether new to me.

senses.head: In total; counting everything
examples: That comes to $45 altogether.
Altogether, about 200 people showed up.

senses.head: On the whole; considering everything
examples: The weather was bad, but altogether it was a good trip.
Altogether, I'd say the meeting went well.

entries.position: before its word — before adjectives (not altogether sure); end with verbs (stop altogether); front for 'in total' and 'on the whole'
entries.modifies: adjectives, verbs, amounts, and whole sentences
entries.form: all + together, written as one word
entries.contrast: Altogether (one word) is 'completely' or 'in total'; all together (two words) is 'everyone in one place or at the same time' (We were all together at Christmas).

entries.meaning: Unselfishly, for the good of others rather than yourself. ---
examples: Most volunteers act altruistically, not for the résumé.
She altruistically gave her bonus to the youngest workers.
Nobody believed the company was behaving altruistically.
entries.position: end — or mid, before the verb
entries.modifies: verbs of acting, giving and helping

entries.meaning: Without skill, like someone who is not a professional. ---
examples: The website looked amateurishly designed.
The robbery was amateurishly planned.
The play was performed amateurishly, but everyone had fun.
entries.position: end — or before a participle (amateurishly made)

entries.meaning: In a way that can be understood in more than one way. ---
examples: The contract was ambiguously worded.
She answered ambiguously, so nobody knew what she meant.
The law is written so ambiguously that lawyers still argue about it.
entries.position: end — or before a participle (ambiguously worded)

entries.meaning: In a way that aims for something big or difficult. ---
examples: The city has ambitiously planned a new light rail system.
The book is ambitiously titled “Everything You Need to Know.”
They started ambitiously but ran out of money within a year.
entries.position: end — or before a participle (ambitiously titled)

entries.meaning: In a pleasant, friendly way. ---
examples: The two men chatted amiably over coffee.
He smiled amiably and offered to help.
The neighbors got along amiably for years.
entries.modifies: verbs of talking, smiling and getting along
entries.contrast: Amiably describes a friendly manner; amicably describes ending a dispute or relationship without a fight (split up amicably).

entries.meaning: Without arguing or fighting; on friendly terms. ---
examples: The dispute was settled amicably out of court.
They divorced amicably and are still friends.
The band split up amicably after ten years.
entries.modifies: verbs like settle, resolve, divorce and split
entries.contrast: Amicably is about settling or ending something without a fight; amiably is simply 'in a friendly manner' (chat amiably).

entries.meaning: Wildly and out of control, in run amok. ---
examples: The kids ran amok while the teacher was out of the room.
Rumors ran amok on social media.
A bull ran amok through the streets of the town.
entries.modifies: the verb run in run amok

entries.meaning: More than enough; fully. ---
examples: Her hard work was amply rewarded.
The results amply demonstrate the need for change.
The kitchen is amply stocked for the weekend.
entries.position: before its word — before participles and verbs (amply rewarded, amply demonstrate)

entries.meaning: In a funny, entertaining way. ---
examples: He told the story amusingly, doing all the voices.
The book is amusingly written.
Amusingly, the fire station's own alarm didn't work.
entries.position: end — or before a participle (amusingly written); front as a comment (Amusingly, …)

entries.meaning: In a similar way; by comparison with a case already mentioned. ---
examples: The second equation can be solved analogously.
Analogously, a city's roads work like the blood vessels in a body.
The new rules apply analogously to part-time employees.
entries.position: end — or front as a linker (Analogously, …)

entries.meaning: By careful, logical analysis. ---
examples: Try to think about the problem analytically.
She approaches every big decision analytically.
The equation can't be solved analytically, only by computer.
entries.modifies: verbs of thinking, approaching and solving

entries.meaning: In terms of the structure of the body. ---
examples: The model of the heart is anatomically correct.
The two species are anatomically very similar.
Anatomically, humans aren't built for sitting all day.
entries.position: before its word — before adjectives (anatomically correct); front with a comma

entries.meaning: And other similar things; and the rest. ---
examples: Bring towels, sunscreen, snacks, and so forth.
We talked about jobs, housing, and so forth.
The form asks for your name, address, and so forth.
entries.position: end — after the last item of a list
entries.contrast: A little more formal than and so on; the two are interchangeable. Do not add etc. after either.

entries.meaning: And other things of the same kind; and the rest. ---
examples: She teaches math, physics, chemistry, and so on.
You still have rent, bills, taxes, and so on.
First one person complained, then another, and so on.
entries.position: end — after the last item of a list
entries.contrast: The everyday form; and so on and so forth is an emphatic spoken version.

entries.meaning: And even more than that. ---
examples: He paid back the loan and then some.
The new model does everything the old one did, and then some.
The renovation will cost fifty thousand dollars and then some.
entries.type: degree — even more than was said
entries.modifies: a statement of amount or quality

entries.meaning: Again, often in a new or different way. ---
examples: After the divorce, she moved to Denver to start life anew.
The debate over gun laws began anew after the shooting.
Every spring the garden comes to life anew.
entries.modifies: verbs like start, begin and come to life

entries.meaning: Sweetly and innocently, like an angel. ---
examples: The baby smiled angelically at us.
The children's choir sang angelically.
She looked up angelically, as if she hadn't eaten the cake.
entries.modifies: verbs of smiling, singing and looking

entries.meaning: In an angry way. ---
examples: “Get out!” he shouted angrily.
She angrily slammed the door.
Protesters reacted angrily to the decision.
entries.position: end — or mid, before the verb

entries.meaning: In a lively, excited way. ---
examples: They were talking animatedly about the game.
She gestured animatedly as she told the story.
The kids chattered animatedly on the bus.

entries.meaning: In a way that annoys you; to an annoying degree. ---
examples: The song was annoyingly catchy.
Annoyingly, the store closed five minutes before we got there.
He's annoyingly good at every sport.
entries.position: before its word — before adjectives; front as a comment (Annoyingly, …)

entries.meaning: Without giving your name. ---
examples: The money was donated anonymously.
You can report the problem anonymously.
The letter was sent anonymously to the newspaper.

entries.meaning: Anxiously has 2 distinct senses.
examples: She looked anxiously at the clock.
Parents waited anxiously for news of the missing hikers.
Fans are anxiously awaiting the band's new album.
The kids have been anxiously counting the days until summer.

senses.head: In a worried, nervous way
examples: She looked anxiously at the clock.
Parents waited anxiously for news of the missing hikers.

senses.head: Eagerly, while waiting for something you want
examples: Fans are anxiously awaiting the band's new album.
The kids have been anxiously counting the days until summer.

entries.position: end — or mid, before the verb
entries.modifies: verbs of waiting, watching and looking

entries.meaning: From now or from then on; anymore. ---
examples: I can't wait any longer.
He doesn't work here any longer.
Nobody uses these phones any longer.
entries.contrast: Used with not or in questions: She doesn't live here any longer. The more formal no longer goes mid-sentence: She no longer lives here. Russian больше не is not not more.

entries.meaning: In or to any place; anywhere. ---
examples: You can sit anyplace you like.
I can't find my glasses anyplace.
Is there anyplace around here that's open this late?
entries.form: any + place, written as one word
entries.contrast: Anyplace is informal American English for anywhere; use anywhere in formal writing. As with anywhere, a negative sentence gives the Russian нигде.

entries.meaning: Anyway: despite that, or to change or return to a topic. ---
examples: Anyways, where was I?
It was raining, but we went anyways.
Anyways, I have to go — talk to you later.
entries.contrast: Anyways belongs to informal American speech; in writing, and in anything formal, use anyway.

entries.meaning: Quickly; at a fast pace. ---
examples: Work on the new stadium continues apace.
Technology is advancing apace.
Construction proceeded apace despite the protests.
entries.type: manner — formal, common in news writing
entries.position: end — usually after continue, proceed or grow

entries.meaning: For each one; each. ---
examples: The tickets cost $20 apiece.
The kids got two cookies apiece.
The houses sold for over a million dollars apiece.
entries.position: after its word — after a price, number or amount
entries.form: a + piece, written as one word

entries.meaning: In a way that shows you are sorry. ---
examples: “I'm so sorry I'm late,” she said apologetically.
He smiled apologetically and moved his bag off the seat.
The waiter shrugged apologetically.
entries.modifies: verbs of speaking, smiling and shrugging

entries.meaning: Shockingly badly; to a shocking degree. ---
examples: The prisoners were treated appallingly.
The hospital was appallingly dirty.
His spelling is appallingly bad for a journalist.
entries.position: before its word — before adjectives; end with verbs

entries.meaning: Appealingly has 2 distinct senses.
examples: The idea is appealingly simple.
The dishes were appealingly arranged on the table.
The puppy looked up at me appealingly.
She glanced appealingly at her father.

senses.head: In an attractive or pleasing way
examples: The idea is appealingly simple.
The dishes were appealingly arranged on the table.

senses.head: In a pleading way, asking for help or sympathy
examples: The puppy looked up at me appealingly.
She glanced appealingly at her father.

entries.position: before its word — before adjectives; end in the 'pleading' sense
entries.modifies: adjectives, participles, and verbs of looking

entries.meaning: Enough to be noticed or measured. ---
examples: Prices haven't changed appreciably in a year.
The new medicine didn't appreciably improve her condition.
The second model is appreciably lighter.
entries.position: before its word — before adjectives and comparatives; end or mid with verbs of change
entries.modifies: adjectives, comparatives, and verbs of change

entries.meaning: In a way that shows you enjoy or are grateful for something. ---
examples: The audience laughed appreciatively.
He sniffed the wine appreciatively.
She nodded appreciatively when I finished explaining.
entries.modifies: verbs of reacting, looking and tasting

entries.meaning: In a worried way, fearing something bad may happen. ---
examples: She looked apprehensively at the dark water.
He opened the envelope apprehensively.
The students waited apprehensively for their grades.
entries.modifies: verbs of looking, waiting and approaching

entries.meaning: In a way that is suitable or right for the situation. ---
examples: Please dress appropriately for the interview.
The hotel is appropriately named Ocean View.
Staff didn't respond appropriately to the complaint.
entries.position: end — or before its word (appropriately dressed); front as a comment (Appropriately, …)

entries.meaning: In a way that shows you think something is good. ---
examples: Her father nodded approvingly.
The crowd murmured approvingly.
He spoke approvingly of the new policy.
entries.modifies: verbs of nodding, smiling and speaking

entries.meaning: A little more or less than; roughly. ---
examples: The flight takes approximately four hours.
Approximately 30 percent of voters are still undecided.
The two paintings were done at approximately the same time.
entries.type: degree — an approximator, more formal than about or around
entries.position: before its word — before numbers, amounts and times
entries.modifies: numbers, amounts, times, and the same

entries.meaning: In a way that fits very well. ---
examples: The town is aptly named Mosquito Creek.
As one critic aptly put it, the movie is all style and no story.
Her boss aptly described the plan as a gamble.
entries.position: before its word — especially before named, described and put
entries.modifies: participles and verbs of naming and describing

entries.meaning: Without a reason or system; by chance or personal whim. ---
examples: The winners were chosen arbitrarily.
The rules seem to be enforced arbitrarily.
He arbitrarily decided to cancel the trip.
entries.position: end — or mid, before the verb

entries.meaning: In terms of architecture or the design of buildings. ---
examples: The building is architecturally significant.
Architecturally, the city is a mix of old and new.
It's one of the most architecturally interesting neighborhoods in Chicago.
entries.position: before its word — before adjectives; front with a comma

entries.meaning: With strong feeling or enthusiasm. ---
examples: She ardently supports animal rights.
He was ardently in love with her.
They argued ardently for a change in the law.
entries.position: mid — before the verb; also end
entries.modifies: verbs of supporting, believing and loving

entries.meaning: All day and all night, without stopping. ---
examples: Doctors worked around the clock during the outbreak.
The store is open around the clock.
Crews are clearing snow around the clock.
entries.contrast: Also an adjective with hyphens: around-the-clock care. British English also says round the clock.

entries.meaning: In a proud way that shows you think you are better than others. ---
examples: He arrogantly assumed he would win.
She dismissed our concerns arrogantly.
The CEO behaved arrogantly toward his staff.
entries.position: end — or mid, before the verb

entries.meaning: Artfully has 2 distinct senses.
examples: The flowers were artfully arranged in a glass vase.
The film artfully mixes comedy and tragedy.
She artfully avoided answering the question.
The report artfully hides how much money was lost.

senses.head: With skill and good taste
examples: The flowers were artfully arranged in a glass vase.
The film artfully mixes comedy and tragedy.

senses.head: In a clever, slightly sly way
examples: She artfully avoided answering the question.
The report artfully hides how much money was lost.

entries.position: end — or before a participle (artfully arranged)

entries.meaning: Clearly and effectively, in well-chosen words. ---
examples: She spoke articulately about her experience.
He explained the problem calmly and articulately.
Few politicians argue as articulately as she does.
entries.modifies: verbs of speaking, writing and explaining

entries.meaning: Not naturally; made or done by people. ---
examples: The drink is artificially sweetened.
Prices are being kept artificially high.
The lake was created artificially in the 1930s.
entries.position: before its word — before adjectives and participles (artificially sweetened); end with verbs

entries.meaning: In an artistic way, or in terms of art. ---
examples: The food was artistically arranged on the plate.
Their daughter is very artistically gifted.
Artistically, the film is a triumph, but it lost money.
entries.русский: художественно, артистично; с художественной точки зрения
entries.position: end — or before its word (artistically gifted); front as a viewpoint (Artistically, …)
entries.modifies: verbs, participles, adjectives, and whole sentences

entries.meaning: In fact; actually, especially when adding something surprising. ---
examples: As a matter of fact, I've never been to New York.
I'm not tired. As a matter of fact, I feel great.
We've met before, as a matter of fact.
entries.type: stance — adds a surprising or correcting fact
entries.contrast: Close to actually and in fact. Russian фактически is closer to in effect or practically.

entries.meaning: Because of what has just been mentioned. ---
examples: The road was closed. As a result, we were an hour late.
He trained all winter and, as a result, won easily.
Sales fell, and two stores closed as a result.
entries.position: front or end — also mid after the subject
entries.contrast: As a result links a sentence to the previous one, so it needs a period or semicolon before it, not just a comma. As a result of + noun is a preposition: as a result of the storm.

entries.meaning: In the way described next. ---
examples: The winners are as follows: Smith, Garcia and Lee.
The recipe goes as follows.
Proceed as follows: open the lid, remove the filter, and rinse it.
entries.modifies: be and verbs of stating, listing or doing
entries.contrast: Always follows, even before a list of many items: The rules are as follows, never as follow.

entries.meaning: As it is has 2 distinct senses.
examples: Don't order more food — we have too much as it is.
I'm late as it is; I can't stop for coffee.
We hoped to finish by May. As it is, we'll be lucky to finish by August.
I wanted to lend him money; as it is, I can barely pay my own bills.

senses.head: Already, even without anything more being added
examples: Don't order more food — we have too much as it is.
I'm late as it is; I can't stop for coffee.

senses.head: In reality, as things actually are, in contrast to what was hoped
examples: We hoped to finish by May. As it is, we'll be lucky to finish by August.
I wanted to lend him money; as it is, I can barely pay my own bills.

entries.русский: и так уже; а на деле
entries.contrast: The literal use means in its present form: Leave the room as it is (как есть). The idiom points to the real situation, often worse than hoped.

entries.meaning: So to speak; shows that a word is not meant literally. ---
examples: He became, as it were, a stranger in his own home.
She's the face of the company, as it were.
We're all in the same boat, as it were.
entries.type: stance — softens an unusual word or image
entries.position: end — or mid, right after the phrase it softens
entries.modifies: a word or phrase used loosely
entries.contrast: A fixed form: never as it was. Slightly formal; it flags a metaphor, like Russian так сказать.

entries.meaning: By chance, whether fortunate or unfortunate. ---
examples: As luck would have it, a taxi was passing just then.
As luck would have it, it rained on the only day we went to the beach.
As luck would have it, my old roommate was the hiring manager.
entries.type: stance — comments on luck, good or bad
entries.contrast: It can go either way; the context decides between к счастью and как назло.

entries.meaning: As such has 2 distinct senses.
examples: There's no fee as such, but you pay for materials.
I'm not a chef as such, but I love to cook.
She is the team leader, and as such she makes the final call.
The house is a landmark and is protected as such.

senses.head: In the exact sense of the word; strictly speaking
examples: There's no fee as such, but you pay for materials.
I'm not a chef as such, but I love to cook.

senses.head: In that role or capacity
examples: She is the team leader, and as such she makes the final call.
The house is a landmark and is protected as such.

entries.type: focusing — the thing itself, in the strict sense
entries.contrast: Careful writers use it only to point back to a noun: He's a guest, and as such he should be treated well. Many Americans now use As such, to mean therefore; editors often mark that wrong.

entries.meaning: In a straight line, not following roads. ---
examples: The town is ten miles away as the crow flies, but twenty by car.
As the crow flies, we live close to the airport.
It's only a mile as the crow flies.
entries.type: place — measured in a straight line

entries.meaning: In the way that usually happens. ---
examples: As usual, he was late.
The store opened at nine as usual.
She ordered the pasta, as usual.
entries.type: manner — the way things usually happen
entries.contrast: Always as usual, never as usually.

entries.meaning: Also; too. ---
examples: Can I get fries as well?
She's a singer, and she writes songs as well.
If you're going, I'll come as well.
entries.contrast: As well goes at the end: I speak French as well. As well as (а также) links to a noun: I speak French as well as Spanish. Might as well means there is no reason not to: We might as well go home.

entries.meaning: Until now; so far. ---
examples: The cause of the fire is as yet unknown.
No one has as yet claimed responsibility.
We have received no reply as yet.
entries.position: mid or end — mid after the auxiliary (has as yet), or end
entries.modifies: verbs, usually negative; un- adjectives (as yet unknown)
entries.contrast: More formal than yet or so far.

entries.meaning: As soon as possible. ---
examples: Please call me back ASAP.
I need those reports ASAP.
Get here ASAP — the meeting's about to start.
entries.form: abbreviation of as soon as possible; said letter by letter or as one word, AY-sap

entries.meaning: Without sex, especially of reproduction in plants and simple organisms. ---
examples: Some plants reproduce asexually.
Bacteria multiply asexually by splitting in two.
Starfish can reproduce both sexually and asexually.

entries.meaning: With suspicion or disapproval. ---
examples: The neighbors looked askance at the new family.
Many doctors still view the treatment askance.
My parents looked askance at my plan to quit college.
entries.type: manner — mostly in look askance at

entries.meaning: Not straight; at an angle. ---
examples: The picture on the wall was hanging askew.
His glasses sat askew after the fall.
She came in with her hat knocked askew by the wind.
entries.position: end — mostly after hang, sit and be

entries.meaning: Asleep has 2 distinct senses.
examples: I fell asleep on the couch watching TV.
The kids were fast asleep by nine.
Try not to fall asleep at the wheel.
My foot fell asleep during the long meeting.
My leg's fallen asleep — give me a second.

senses.head: Into or in a state of sleep
examples: I fell asleep on the couch watching TV.
The kids were fast asleep by nine.
Try not to fall asleep at the wheel.

senses.head: Of an arm or leg: numb from pressure
examples: My foot fell asleep during the long meeting.
My leg's fallen asleep — give me a second.

entries.position: end — after fall, be and stay
entries.contrast: In The baby is asleep it works like an adjective, but it never goes before a noun: a sleeping baby, not an asleep baby.

entries.meaning: In a confident, forceful way that makes others listen. ---
examples: She learned to speak assertively in meetings.
If the landlord ignores you, follow up assertively in writing.
He assertively pushed for a raise.

entries.meaning: With great care and steady effort. ---
examples: She assiduously avoided talking about her past.
The staff worked assiduously to keep the records accurate.
He had assiduously built a reputation for honesty.

entries.meaning: Certainly; without doubt. ---
examples: This is assuredly not the last we'll hear of it.
"Will you be there?" "Most assuredly."
The new rules will assuredly face a legal challenge.
entries.position: mid — also alone in most assuredly

entries.meaning: In a way that causes great surprise; to a surprising degree. ---
examples: Astonishingly, no one was hurt in the crash.
The results were astonishingly good.
She learned the language astonishingly fast.
entries.type: stance — a comment on the sentence; also degree
entries.position: front — as a comment; before an adjective or adverb as a degree word

entries.meaning: To an extremely high degree, especially of prices or numbers. ---
examples: Rents in the city have risen astronomically.
The odds against it are astronomically high.
Tuition has gone up astronomically since the 1980s.
entries.position: before its word — astronomically high; also end
entries.modifies: adjectives, and verbs of rising and costing

entries.meaning: In a sharp, clever way that shows good judgment. ---
examples: She astutely noticed the error in the contract.
As one critic astutely pointed out, the plan had no budget.
He invested astutely and retired early.

entries.meaning: In a way that is not the same on both sides. ---
examples: The building was designed asymmetrically, with one tall tower.
Her hair was cut asymmetrically, longer on the left.
The weight was distributed asymmetrically, so the shelf tipped over.

entries.meaning: For less money than it cost. ---
examples: They had to sell the house at a loss.
The store has been operating at a loss for two years.
Airlines often fly these routes at a loss.
entries.modifies: verbs of selling, running and operating
entries.contrast: After be, at a loss usually means puzzled: I'm at a loss for words (не знаю, что сказать) — an adjective use. The business opposite is at a profit.

entries.meaning: Together in one group, or in one stretch without stopping. ---
examples: Please come in one at a time.
He ran up the stairs two steps at a time.
She sometimes works for twelve hours at a time.
entries.position: end — after a number (one at a time)
entries.contrast: At a time counts things together: two at a time (по двое). At one time means formerly, and at times means sometimes.

entries.meaning: In any way; to any degree. ---
examples: I didn't sleep at all last night.
Do you speak any Russian at all?
If you have any questions at all, just call.
entries.type: degree — strengthens a negative or question
entries.position: end — or right after the negative word (not at all)
entries.contrast: Only with negatives, questions and if: I don't like it at all, never I like it at all. Not at all is also a polite reply to thanks.

entries.meaning: Whatever it takes; no matter what the price or sacrifice. ---
examples: The general wanted to win at all costs.
Avoid that highway at all costs during rush hour.
The secret must be kept at all costs.
entries.contrast: Always plural costs in this form; the singular version is at any cost.

entries.meaning: At any rate has 2 distinct senses.
examples: I'm not sure who won. At any rate, it's over.
At any rate, we should get going.
He's a good teacher — at any rate, the students like him.
It was a success, or at any rate not a disaster.

senses.head: Anyway; used to move on or return to the main point
examples: I'm not sure who won. At any rate, it's over.
At any rate, we should get going.

senses.head: At least; used to correct or limit what was just said
examples: He's a good teacher — at any rate, the students like him.
It was a success, or at any rate not a disaster.

entries.русский: во всяком случае; по крайней мере

entries.meaning: At a safe distance; without getting close, physically or personally. ---
examples: She keeps her coworkers at arm's length.
The senator kept the lobbyists at arm's length.
He held the dirty sock at arm's length.
entries.type: manner — at a distance, not letting someone close
entries.contrast: In business, an arm's-length deal is one between independent parties with no special relationship.

entries.meaning: Even in the most favorable view; no better than. ---
examples: The plan is risky at best.
We'll break even this year, at best.
At best, the repairs will take a week.
entries.type: degree — limits a statement to the most favorable case
entries.position: front or end — or right before the word it limits
entries.modifies: a clause, an adjective, or a number
entries.contrast: The opposite is at worst. At the best of times is a separate phrase: He's grumpy at the best of times (даже в хорошие дни).

entries.meaning: From very near. ---
examples: The victim was shot at close range.
We watched the whales at close range.
Seen at close range, the moon rock looked like ordinary gravel.
entries.modifies: verbs of shooting, seeing and watching

entries.meaning: At the beginning, in contrast with what happened later. ---
examples: At first I didn't like the city.
It was hard at first, but it got easier.
At first she thought it was a joke.
entries.contrast: At first always implies that something changed later. To order steps or points, use first or firstly: ✗ At first, preheat the oven → First, preheat the oven. Russian сначала covers both, which is why the error is so common.

entries.meaning: When first considered; on first impression. ---
examples: At first blush, the offer seems generous.
The idea sounds crazy at first blush.
At first blush, the two cases look alike.
entries.type: viewpoint — a first impression that may change
entries.contrast: More bookish than at first glance; nothing to do with blushing.

entries.meaning: When first seen, before looking closely. ---
examples: At first glance, the problem looks simple.
The two paintings look identical at first glance.
At first glance, it's an ordinary house.
entries.type: viewpoint — a first impression that may change
entries.contrast: For a first impression Americans usually say at first glance; at first sight is mostly love at first sight.

entries.meaning: At first sight has 2 distinct senses.
examples: It was love at first sight.
He recognized her at first sight.
At first sight, the job looked easy.
The theory seems convincing at first sight.

senses.head: The moment someone or something is first seen
examples: It was love at first sight.
He recognized her at first sight.

senses.head: On first impression, before looking closely
examples: At first sight, the job looked easy.
The theory seems convincing at first sight.

entries.русский: с первого взгляда; на первый взгляд
entries.position: end — or front for the first-impression sense
entries.modifies: verbs of loving and recognizing; a whole clause
entries.contrast: Its most common use is love at first sight (любовь с первого взгляда). For a first impression at first glance is more usual.

entries.meaning: In one's real nature; basically. ---
examples: He's a kind man at heart.
She's still a small-town girl at heart.
At heart, the book is a love story.
entries.type: viewpoint — what someone really is inside
entries.position: mid or end — after be, or at the end
entries.modifies: be with a noun or adjective; a whole clause
entries.contrast: Different from by heart (наизусть). Have someone's interests at heart means to care about them.

entries.meaning: At home has 2 distinct senses.
examples: I left my phone at home.
She works at home on Fridays.
Will you be at home tonight?
The president is popular abroad but not at home.
The company sells more overseas than at home.

senses.head: In one's own house
examples: I left my phone at home.
She works at home on Fridays.
Will you be at home tonight?

senses.head: In one's own country, not abroad
examples: The president is popular abroad but not at home.
The company sells more overseas than at home.

entries.contrast: Americans often drop at after stay and be: stay home, Is Mom home? After a verb of motion there is never at: go home, not go at home. Feel at home and Make yourself at home mean comfortable, as in one's own house (как дома).

entries.meaning: At large has 2 distinct senses.
examples: The escaped prisoner is still at large.
Police warned that the gunman remained at large.
The decision will affect society at large.
The public at large knows little about the issue.

senses.head: Free and not yet caught, of a criminal or animal
examples: The escaped prisoner is still at large.
Police warned that the gunman remained at large.

senses.head: As a whole; in general, after a noun
examples: The decision will affect society at large.
The public at large knows little about the issue.

entries.type: manner — free and not caught; also, after a noun, as a whole
entries.position: after its word — after be or remain, or after a noun (society at large)
entries.modifies: be, remain; nouns for groups of people
entries.contrast: Not largely (в основном). In American politics a member at large represents a whole city or state, not one district.

entries.meaning: After a long time or much waiting. ---
examples: At last, the rain stopped.
We're home at last!
She had found a job she loved at last.
entries.contrast: At last follows a long wait and shows relief. For the final item in a list use finally or lastly: Finally, add the salt, not At last, add the salt.

entries.meaning: At least has 2 distinct senses.
examples: The trip takes at least three hours.
She must be at least sixty.
Drink at least eight glasses of water a day.
The food was bad, but at least it was cheap.
Call her, or at least send a text.

senses.head: Not less than; possibly more
examples: The trip takes at least three hours.
She must be at least sixty.
Drink at least eight glasses of water a day.

senses.head: Anyway; used to point out something good, or to limit what was said
examples: The food was bad, but at least it was cheap.
Call her, or at least send a text.

entries.русский: не меньше; по крайней мере, хотя бы
entries.position: before its word — before a number; front or mid as a comment
entries.modifies: numbers and amounts; a whole clause
entries.contrast: As a comment it often points to something good in a bad situation: At least nobody was hurt (хорошо хоть). At the least is a rarer variant.

entries.meaning: At length has 2 distinct senses.
examples: The professor spoke at length about the causes of the war.
We discussed the plan at length.
At length, the door opened.
At length he agreed to see a doctor.

senses.head: For a long time and in great detail
examples: The professor spoke at length about the causes of the war.
We discussed the plan at length.

senses.head: After a long time; finally
examples: At length, the door opened.
At length he agreed to see a doctor.

entries.position: end — or front in the finally sense
entries.modifies: verbs of speaking, writing and discussing
entries.contrast: The finally sense is literary; in everyday American English at length almost always means for a long time, in detail.

entries.meaning: Finally, after a very long wait. ---
examples: At long last, the bridge is open.
The package arrived at long last.
At long last, she got the recognition she deserved.
entries.contrast: A stronger, more emotional at last.

entries.meaning: Not more than; possibly less. ---
examples: The walk takes twenty minutes at most.
There were at most a dozen people in the audience.
At most, you'll pay a small fine.
entries.position: before its word — before a number; or end (twenty minutes at most)
entries.modifies: numbers and amounts; a whole clause
entries.contrast: At the most is a common spoken variant. Not mostly (в основном).

entries.meaning: At once has 2 distinct senses.
examples: Come here at once!
The doctor saw him at once.
I knew at once that something was wrong.
Don't all talk at once.
I can't do three things at once.

senses.head: Immediately; without delay
examples: Come here at once!
The doctor saw him at once.
I knew at once that something was wrong.

senses.head: At the same time; together
examples: Don't all talk at once.
I can't do three things at once.

entries.contrast: At once (немедленно) is more formal than right away. All at once usually means suddenly. For a single occasion say once: I went there once.

entries.meaning: At one time has 2 distinct senses.
examples: At one time, this town had three movie theaters.
She was at one time the best player on the team.
The elevator holds only eight people at one time.
Don't take more than two pills at one time.

senses.head: In the past; formerly
examples: At one time, this town had three movie theaters.
She was at one time the best player on the team.

senses.head: Together; at the same time
examples: The elevator holds only eight people at one time.
Don't take more than two pills at one time.

entries.position: any position — front, mid after be, or end
entries.contrast: At one time meaning formerly (когда-то) is not at once (сразу).

entries.meaning: Now; at this time. ---
examples: At present, there are no plans to close the school.
The position is not available at present.
We have about 200 employees at present.
entries.contrast: More formal than at the moment or right now. No article: at present, not at the present.

entries.meaning: Without a plan, choice or pattern. ---
examples: The winners will be chosen at random.
He opened the book at random and began to read.
The attacker seemed to pick victims at random.
entries.contrast: The one-word adverb is randomly. In slang the adjective random also means strange or unexpected.

entries.meaning: At risk; able to be lost or won, depending on the outcome. ---
examples: Thousands of jobs are at stake.
With so much money at stake, nobody wants to make a mistake.
Her reputation was at stake.
entries.type: manner — describes what may be won or lost
entries.position: after its word — after be, or after a noun (the money at stake)
entries.modifies: be; nouns for what can be lost
entries.contrast: Spelled stake, not steak. Close to at risk, but at risk usually means danger to people or things.

entries.meaning: Now; at the present time. ---
examples: She's in a meeting at the moment.
At the moment we have no plans to move.
I'm not working at the moment.
entries.contrast: At the moment means now; in a moment means soon; in the moment means fully focused on the present. Usually with a present tense, often the present progressive.

entries.meaning: At the same time has 2 distinct senses.
examples: We both started talking at the same time.
You can't text and drive at the same time.
I want to help him. At the same time, I don't want to be used.
The job pays well; at the same time, the hours are terrible.

senses.head: Together; simultaneously
examples: We both started talking at the same time.
You can't text and drive at the same time.

senses.head: However; on the other hand
body: (в то же время, вместе с тем)
examples: I want to help him. At the same time, I don't want to be used.
The job pays well; at the same time, the hours are terrible.

entries.position: front or end — front with a comma in the linking sense
entries.contrast: In the linking sense it introduces a contrasting fact, not a time — like Russian вместе с тем.

entries.meaning: Sometimes; occasionally. ---
examples: At times, I wonder if I made the right choice.
The road can be dangerous at times.
He can be difficult at times.
entries.contrast: Not at a time (за раз) or at one time (когда-то).

entries.meaning: Whenever or however one wants. ---
examples: The cat comes and goes at will.
Users can change the settings at will.
He seemed able to cry at will.
entries.contrast: In US law, at-will employment means either side can end the job at any time without giving a reason.

entries.meaning: In the worst possible case. ---
examples: At worst, we'll have to start over.
The side effects are mild at worst.
His remarks were careless at best and dishonest at worst.
entries.type: degree — limits a statement to the least favorable case
entries.contrast: The opposite of at best, and often paired with it: careless at best, dishonest at worst.

entries.meaning: Very badly; in a shockingly bad or cruel way. ---
examples: The team played atrociously in the second half.
The prisoners were treated atrociously.
The service at that restaurant is atrociously slow.
entries.position: end — also before its word as a degree word

entries.meaning: With close attention. ---
examples: The students listened attentively to the speaker.
She watched attentively as the chef sliced the fish.
The nurses cared for him attentively day and night.

entries.meaning: In a way that is pleasing to look at or appealing. ---
examples: The dishes were attractively arranged on the table.
The house is attractively priced for the neighborhood.
She dressed attractively but simply.
entries.position: end — also before a past participle: attractively priced

entries.meaning: In a way that is not typical or usual. ---
examples: It was atypically warm for February.
Atypically, the boss arrived late and said nothing.
The patient responded atypically to the drug.
entries.position: before its word — mostly an adjective; also front, as a comment

entries.meaning: In a bold, daring way that ignores risk or convention. ---
examples: The thieves audaciously robbed the bank in broad daylight.
She audaciously asked the CEO for his job.
The museum was audaciously designed, with no straight walls.

entries.meaning: Loudly enough to be heard. ---
examples: He sighed audibly when the meeting ran late.
Please speak audibly so the back row can hear you.
The audience gasped audibly.

entries.meaning: In a way that suggests future success. ---
examples: The season began auspiciously with three straight wins.
Their partnership started auspiciously.
The trip didn't begin auspiciously — we missed our flight.

entries.meaning: In a plain, strict way, with no comfort or decoration. ---
examples: The monks' rooms were austerely furnished.
She lived austerely on a small pension.
The chapel was austerely beautiful, with bare stone walls.
entries.position: before its word — mostly a past participle: austerely furnished; also end

entries.meaning: In a real, genuine, or true-to-the-original way. ---
examples: The restaurant serves authentically Mexican food.
It's hard to act authentically on camera.
The film authentically recreates 1960s Detroit.
entries.position: end — also mid, and before an adjective

entries.meaning: With confidence and expert knowledge, in a way people trust. ---
examples: She spoke authoritatively about climate policy.
No one can say authoritatively what caused the fire.
He answered authoritatively, as if he'd been there.

entries.meaning: With total power, ignoring what others think. ---
examples: The founder ran the company autocratically for decades.
He governed autocratically and jailed his critics.
Don't make decisions autocratically — ask the team.

entries.meaning: Automatically has 2 distinct senses.
examples: The doors open automatically when you walk up to them.
If you pay late, a fee is added automatically.
The app saves your work automatically every five minutes.
I automatically reached for my phone when I woke up.
She said thank you automatically, without looking up.

senses.head: By itself, without a person controlling it; or as a fixed result of something
examples: The doors open automatically when you walk up to them.
If you pay late, a fee is added automatically.
