The app saves your work automatically every five minutes.

senses.head: Without thinking about it
examples: I automatically reached for my phone when I woke up.
She said thank you automatically, without looking up.

entries.meaning: With great eagerness and interest. ---
examples: She avidly reads every mystery novel she can find.
He followed the election results avidly.
As a kid, I avidly collected baseball cards.

entries.meaning: Very; extremely. ---
examples: It's awful cold out there this morning.
That's an awful big dog for such a small apartment.
She seemed awful tired when she got home.
entries.form: flat — the same form as the adjective awful
entries.contrast: Informal spoken American; careful writing uses awfully (awfully cold). In an awful lot, awful is an adjective describing lot.

entries.meaning: For a short time. ---
examples: Why don't you stay awhile and have some coffee?
Let's sit here awhile and rest.
The kids played outside awhile before dinner.
entries.contrast: Write awhile as one word only with no preposition before it (stay awhile). After for or in, write two words: for a while, in a while.

entries.meaning: Awkwardly has 2 distinct senses.
examples: He danced awkwardly at the wedding.
She fell awkwardly and twisted her ankle.
They stood awkwardly in silence after the argument.
The meeting ended awkwardly when no one knew what to say.
He laughed awkwardly at the boss's joke.

senses.head: In a clumsy way, without ease or grace
examples: He danced awkwardly at the wedding.
She fell awkwardly and twisted her ankle.

senses.head: In an embarrassing or uncomfortable way
examples: They stood awkwardly in silence after the argument.
The meeting ended awkwardly when no one knew what to say.
He laughed awkwardly at the boss's joke.

entries.meaning: Awry has 2 distinct senses.
examples: Something went awry during the launch.
Their plans for the weekend went badly awry.
His tie was awry after the long day.
The wind had blown her hair awry.

senses.head: Away from what was planned or expected; wrong
examples: Something went awry during the launch.
Their plans for the weekend went badly awry.

senses.head: Out of the normal or correct position; crooked
examples: His tie was awry after the long day.
The wind had blown her hair awry.

entries.meaning: Before the traditional date of the birth of Christ, used after a year. ---
examples: Julius Caesar was killed in 44 B.C.
The temple was built around 500 B.C.
The city was founded in the eighth century B.C.
entries.position: after its word — after the year or century
entries.form: abbreviation of before Christ; also written BC
entries.contrast: B.C. goes after the year (44 B.C.), but A.D. traditionally goes before it (A.D. 79). Scholarly and neutral writing often uses B.C.E. and C.E. instead.

entries.meaning: Before the Common Era; the same years as B.C., used after a year. ---
examples: The Great Pyramid was built around 2560 B.C.E.
Confucius was born in 551 B.C.E.
The clay tablets date from the third millennium B.C.E.
entries.position: after its word — after the year or century
entries.form: abbreviation of before the Common Era; also written BCE

entries.meaning: From one place or side to another and back again, repeatedly. ---
examples: He paced back and forth across the room.
We emailed back and forth for weeks.
The kids ran back and forth between the two houses.
entries.modifies: verbs of moving, talking and writing
entries.contrast: Americans say back and forth; backwards and forwards is more British. Also a noun: the back-and-forth of the negotiations.

entries.meaning: In or into the area behind a theater stage. ---
examples: We went backstage to meet the band after the show.
The actors were waiting nervously backstage.
Reporters aren't allowed backstage during the ceremony.

entries.meaning: Backwards has 2 distinct senses.
examples: She took a step backwards and tripped over the cat.
He fell backwards into the pool.
The car started rolling backwards down the hill.
Can you say the alphabet backwards?
You've got your sweater on backwards.
Count backwards from ten.

senses.head: Toward the back; in the direction behind you
examples: She took a step backwards and tripped over the cat.
He fell backwards into the pool.
The car started rolling backwards down the hill.

senses.head: In reverse order, or with the back part in front
examples: Can you say the alphabet backwards?
You've got your sweater on backwards.
Count backwards from ten.

entries.contrast: American English uses both backward and backwards as adverbs, and careful writing leans to backward; British English prefers backwards. Only backward is an adjective: a backward glance.

entries.meaning: Very much; seriously. ---
examples: I need a vacation so bad.
He got hurt pretty bad in the crash.
Nobody wanted that job worse than she did.
entries.modifies: verbs, especially want, need and hurt
entries.form: flat — the same form as the adjective bad
entries.contrast: Informal spoken American; careful writing uses badly (badly hurt). After linking verbs bad is an adjective and correct in any style: I feel bad, not I feel badly.

entries.meaning: In a plain, direct way, with nothing to soften it. ---
examples: "You're fired," he said baldly.
To put it baldly, we're out of money.
The report baldly states that the bridge is unsafe.
entries.position: end — mostly with say, state or put
entries.form: -ly from bald in its sense plain

entries.meaning: On a horse without a saddle. ---
examples: She learned to ride bareback on her grandfather's farm.
The kids rode the pony bareback around the field.
Riding bareback takes good balance.
entries.form: flat — the same form as the adjective bareback

entries.meaning: Without shoes or socks. ---
examples: The children ran barefoot along the beach.
Don't walk around barefoot — there's broken glass.
He came to the door barefoot and half asleep.
entries.form: flat — the same form as the adjective barefoot; barefooted also exists

entries.meaning: In a shy, easily embarrassed way. ---
examples: She smiled bashfully when he complimented her.
The boy looked down bashfully at his shoes.
He bashfully admitted he had written the poem.

entries.meaning: In a beautiful way; very well. ---
examples: She sings beautifully.
The old house has been beautifully restored.
The new plan worked beautifully.
entries.position: end — also before a past participle: beautifully restored

entries.meaning: Soon; after a short time. ---
examples: Before long, the whole town knew.
You'll be walking again before long.
It got dark before long, and we headed back.
entries.contrast: Not long before (задолго до): Before long he left (вскоре ушёл) vs long before he left (задолго до его ухода).

entries.meaning: Later than it should have happened. ---
examples: The company belatedly apologized for the data leak.
He belatedly realized he'd left his wallet at home.
I wished her a happy birthday belatedly, two days after.

entries.meaning: In a way that can be believed; convincingly. ---
examples: The actor plays a doctor very believably.
The characters are believably drawn.
She lied believably enough to fool the police.

entries.meaning: In an angry, aggressive way, ready to fight. ---
examples: He belligerently refused to show his ID.
The drunk customer shouted belligerently at the staff.
She stared belligerently at anyone who questioned her.

entries.meaning: Unfairly, especially by attacking someone's weak point. ---
examples: Bringing up his divorce in the debate was hitting below the belt.
That comment was a little below the belt.
The campaign ads went below the belt.

entries.meaning: In a kind, well-meaning way, often from a position of power. ---
examples: The old man smiled benevolently at the children.
By most accounts, the king ruled benevolently.
She looked on benevolently as the students celebrated.

entries.meaning: In a kind, gentle, harmless way. ---
examples: The professor smiled benignly at the nervous student.
The dog looked up benignly from its bed.
The policy was benignly intended but caused real harm.

entries.meaning: Most pleasing of all the things mentioned. ---
examples: The hotel is clean, cheap and, best of all, right on the beach.
Best of all, the tickets are free.
I like all her books, but I like this one best of all.
entries.position: front — usually before the last item
entries.modifies: a whole clause, or the last item of a list
entries.contrast: The opposite is worst of all.

entries.meaning: In the space or time that separates two things. ---
examples: There's a hotel at each end of the street and shops in between.
The two storms hit a week apart, with sunny days in between.
Good restaurants are few and far between in this town.
entries.contrast: Usually a preposition with an object (between the two houses). It is an adverb when the object is left out: two houses with a garden in between.

entries.meaning: To a degree that confuses you. ---
examples: The tax rules are bewilderingly complex.
The menu offered a bewilderingly long list of options.
Prices changed bewilderingly fast that year.
entries.position: before its word — mostly an adjective

entries.meaning: Beyond has 2 distinct senses.
examples: From the porch you can see the lake and the mountains beyond.
The road ends at the gate, and there's only desert beyond.
The plan covers the next five years and beyond.
Kids in third grade and beyond can join the club.

senses.head: Farther away; on the far side
examples: From the porch you can see the lake and the mountains beyond.
The road ends at the gate, and there's only desert beyond.

senses.head: Later in time or further in amount; after that
examples: The plan covers the next five years and beyond.
Kids in third grade and beyond can join the club.

entries.contrast: Usually a preposition (beyond the river, beyond belief). It is an adverb when nothing follows it: the hills beyond, 2030 and beyond.

entries.term: beyond a shadow of a doubt
entries.respell: bi-yahnd uh shad-oh uhv uh DOWT
entries.meaning: With complete certainty. ---
examples: The DNA proved beyond a shadow of a doubt that he was there.
I knew beyond a shadow of a doubt that she was the one.
Beyond a shadow of a doubt, this is his best album.
entries.modifies: verbs of knowing and proving; a whole clause
entries.contrast: The legal standard is beyond a reasonable doubt, which is weaker.

entries.meaning: So certainly that no one can question it. ---
examples: His honesty is beyond doubt.
The tests proved beyond doubt that the water was safe.
It is now beyond doubt that the painting is a fake.
entries.position: end — usually after be or a verb of proving
entries.modifies: be; verbs of proving and showing
entries.contrast: Formal. Speech prefers without a doubt; no doubt often means only probably.

entries.meaning: Extremely; more than can be measured. ---
examples: She was grateful beyond measure.
His music has enriched our lives beyond measure.
The war caused suffering beyond measure.
entries.position: after its word — after an adjective or verb

entries.meaning: Twice a year. ---
examples: The committee meets biannually, in March and September.
The newsletter is published biannually.
Prices are reviewed biannually.
entries.contrast: Biannually means twice a year; biennially means every two years. Readers often confuse them, so when it matters, write twice a year or every two years.

entries.meaning: Once every two years. ---
examples: The art festival is held biennially.
The license must be renewed biennially.
Elections for the board take place biennially.
entries.contrast: Biennially means every two years; biannually means twice a year. When it matters, write every two years or twice a year.

entries.meaning: Big has 2 distinct senses.
examples: If you want to grow the business, you have to think big.
She won big at the poker table last night.
Next year, we're going to dream even bigger.
He talks big, but he never follows through.
Don't talk big if you can't back it up.

senses.head: On a large scale; ambitiously or with great success
examples: If you want to grow the business, you have to think big.
She won big at the poker table last night.
Next year, we're going to dream even bigger.

senses.head: In a boastful way
examples: He talks big, but he never follows through.
Don't talk big if you can't back it up.

entries.position: end — after think, win, talk and dream
entries.modifies: a few verbs: think, win, talk, dream
entries.form: flat — the same form as the adjective big
entries.contrast: Informal and limited to a few verbs. In a big win or a big dream, big is an adjective.

entries.meaning: Between two sides, especially two countries. ---
examples: The two countries agreed to settle the dispute bilaterally.
Trade issues are often handled bilaterally rather than through the UN.
The deal was negotiated bilaterally, without the rest of the alliance.

entries.meaning: In two languages. ---
examples: Their kids are being raised bilingually, in English and Russian.
The school teaches math and science bilingually.
All the signs at the airport are printed bilingually.

entries.meaning: Every two months, or sometimes twice a month. ---
examples: The magazine is published bimonthly.
The club meets bimonthly, in odd-numbered months.
We pay the water bill bimonthly.
entries.русский: раз в два месяца; дважды в месяц
entries.contrast: Ambiguous: it usually means every two months but sometimes twice a month. If the difference matters, write every other month or twice a month. Also an adjective: a bimonthly magazine.

entries.meaning: Gradually; a little at a time. ---
examples: Bit by bit, the town was rebuilt.
He paid off the debt bit by bit.
She's getting her strength back bit by bit.

entries.meaning: Bitingly has 2 distinct senses.
examples: She commented bitingly on his lack of experience.
The review was bitingly funny.
It was bitingly cold on the ski lift.
A bitingly cold wind blew off the river.

senses.head: In a sharp, sarcastic way meant to hurt
examples: She commented bitingly on his lack of experience.
The review was bitingly funny.

senses.head: Extremely, of cold or wind
examples: It was bitingly cold on the ski lift.
A bitingly cold wind blew off the river.

entries.position: end — also before its word: bitingly cold

entries.meaning: Extremely, of cold weather. ---
examples: It was bitter cold on the morning of the parade.
The wind off the lake gets bitter cold in January.
Chicago can stay bitter cold for weeks at a time.
entries.form: flat — the same form as the adjective bitter
entries.contrast: Only in bitter cold. Elsewhere bitter is an adjective: bitter coffee, a bitter fight.

entries.meaning: Every two weeks. ---
examples: Most employees here are paid biweekly.
The team meets biweekly on Tuesdays.
The newsletter goes out biweekly.
entries.contrast: In American usage it almost always means every two weeks (paid biweekly), but it can also mean twice a week; every other week is unambiguous. Also an adjective: a biweekly paycheck.

entries.meaning: In a calm, mild way that shows no strong feeling or interest. ---
examples: "That's not my problem," the clerk said blandly.
He smiled blandly and changed the subject.
The press release blandly described the layoffs as a restructuring.

entries.meaning: With no expression, often because you do not understand. ---
examples: She stared blankly at the math problem.
He looked at me blankly when I mentioned the meeting.
The students gazed blankly at the board.
entries.position: end — mostly after stare and look

entries.meaning: In an obvious and shameless way. ---
examples: The ad was blatantly misleading.
He blatantly ignored the stop sign.
That's a blatantly false statement.
entries.position: before its word — blatantly false; also mid

entries.meaning: In a cold, gloomy, or hopeless way. ---
examples: "We'll never get out of here," he said bleakly.
She stared bleakly out at the rain.
The report bleakly predicts more job losses.

entries.meaning: In a welcome way that brings relief. ---
examples: The house was blessedly quiet after the kids left.
Blessedly, the rain stopped before the ceremony.
The drive home was blessedly short.
entries.type: degree — with a sense of relief; also stance
entries.position: before its word — blessedly quiet; also front

entries.meaning: Blindly has 2 distinct senses.
examples: He felt around blindly for the light switch.
She ran blindly through the smoke.
Don't blindly trust everything you read online.
The soldiers followed orders blindly.
He blindly accepted the first offer.

senses.head: Without being able to see
examples: He felt around blindly for the light switch.
She ran blindly through the smoke.

senses.head: Without thinking or asking questions
examples: Don't blindly trust everything you read online.
The soldiers followed orders blindly.
He blindly accepted the first offer.

entries.meaning: In a completely happy or untroubled way. ---
examples: They were blissfully unaware of the storm coming their way.
The baby slept blissfully through the noise.
The newlyweds seemed blissfully happy.
entries.position: before its word — blissfully happy, blissfully unaware; also end

entries.meaning: In a casual, careless way, without noticing or caring about problems. ---
examples: He blithely ignored the warning signs.
She blithely assumed someone else would pay.
The company blithely promised results it couldn't deliver.

entries.meaning: In a direct, honest way, without trying to be polite. ---
examples: She told him bluntly that his work wasn't good enough.
To put it bluntly, we can't afford it.
The doctor spoke bluntly about the risks.
entries.type: manner; also viewpoint in to put it bluntly
entries.position: end — also front in to put it bluntly

entries.meaning: In a way that shows too much pride in yourself. ---
examples: He talked boastfully about his new car.
"I've never lost a match," she said boastfully.
The ad boastfully claimed to be the best in town.

entries.meaning: By taking hold of the whole body; by physical force. ---
examples: The bouncer picked him up bodily and carried him out.
She was lifted bodily from the wreck.
The two protesters were removed bodily from the meeting.
entries.position: end — after verbs of lifting and moving
entries.contrast: More often an adjective: bodily harm, bodily fluids.

entries.meaning: Extremely; used only in boiling hot. ---
examples: The coffee was boiling hot.
It gets boiling hot in the attic by noon.
Don't touch the pan — it's still boiling hot.
entries.form: the -ing form of boil, used as a degree word

entries.meaning: In a loud, energetic, and cheerful way. ---
examples: The fans cheered boisterously after the goal.
The kids played boisterously in the backyard.
They laughed boisterously at the next table.

entries.meaning: In a brave, confident way that takes risks. ---
examples: She boldly asked for a promotion in her first month.
The company moved boldly into new markets.
The walls were boldly painted in red and orange.

entries.meaning: Completely straight; used only in bolt upright. ---
examples: She sat bolt upright in bed when the phone rang.
He stood bolt upright as the general walked in.
The crash made everyone sit bolt upright.
entries.contrast: Only in bolt upright. Elsewhere bolt is a noun (a bolt of lightning) or a verb (The horse bolted).

entries.meaning: In a rude, crude way, with no regard for other people. ---
examples: He behaved boorishly at the dinner party.
A few fans acted boorishly, yelling insults at the players' families.
She was tired of tourists who boorishly ignored the museum rules.

entries.meaning: In a dull, uninteresting way. ---
examples: The movie was boringly predictable.
He spoke boringly for an hour about tax law.
The plan is boringly simple, and that's why it works.
entries.position: before its word — boringly predictable; also end

entries.meaning: In a way typical of a boy; young and charming. ---
examples: He grinned boyishly when she laughed.
At fifty, he was still boyishly handsome.
The senator boyishly ran a hand through his hair.
entries.position: end — also before an adjective: boyishly handsome

entries.meaning: In a loud, overconfident way. ---
examples: The young CEO brashly predicted he'd beat Amazon.
He spoke brashly about winning the title.
She brashly ignored the advice of more experienced colleagues.

entries.meaning: In a way that shows courage. ---
examples: The firefighters bravely entered the burning building.
She fought the illness bravely for years.
He smiled bravely, though he was clearly in pain.

entries.meaning: In an open, shameless way, without embarrassment. ---
examples: The thief brazenly walked out with a TV in broad daylight.
He brazenly lied to the judge.
Some drivers brazenly run red lights.

entries.meaning: Breathlessly has 2 distinct senses.
examples: She ran up the stairs and arrived breathlessly at the door.
"I made it," he said breathlessly.
Fans waited breathlessly for the announcement.
The press reported breathlessly on every detail of the wedding.

senses.head: While out of breath
examples: She ran up the stairs and arrived breathlessly at the door.
"I made it," he said breathlessly.

senses.head: With great excitement or eagerness
examples: Fans waited breathlessly for the announcement.
The press reported breathlessly on every detail of the wedding.

entries.meaning: In a cheerful, relaxed, casual way. ---
examples: "Don't worry about it," she said breezily.
He breezily dismissed the criticism.
The book is breezily written and easy to read.

entries.meaning: With a lot of light. ---
examples: The stars were shining bright over the desert.
The fire burned brighter as the wind picked up.
We have to be up bright and early tomorrow.
entries.modifies: shine, burn, and early in bright and early
entries.form: flat — the same form as the adjective bright
entries.contrast: Only after shine and burn, and in bright and early. Elsewhere use brightly: she smiled brightly.

entries.meaning: Brightly has 2 distinct senses.
examples: The sun was shining brightly.
The room was brightly painted in yellow and blue.
The store windows were brightly lit.
"Good morning!" she said brightly.
He smiled brightly at the new neighbors.

senses.head: With a lot of light or strong color
examples: The sun was shining brightly.
The room was brightly painted in yellow and blue.
The store windows were brightly lit.

senses.head: In a cheerful, lively way
examples: "Good morning!" she said brightly.
He smiled brightly at the new neighbors.

entries.position: end — also before a past participle: brightly lit

entries.meaning: Brilliantly has 2 distinct senses.
examples: She played the role brilliantly.
The plan worked brilliantly.
He brilliantly solved the problem in minutes.
The stars shone brilliantly in the desert sky.
The trees were full of brilliantly colored birds.

senses.head: Extremely well; with great skill
examples: She played the role brilliantly.
The plan worked brilliantly.
He brilliantly solved the problem in minutes.

senses.head: With very bright light or color
examples: The stars shone brilliantly in the desert sky.
The trees were full of brilliantly colored birds.

entries.meaning: In a quick, energetic way. ---
examples: We walked briskly to stay warm.
Tickets sold briskly after the announcement.
"Let's get started," she said briskly.

entries.meaning: Broadly has 2 distinct senses.
examples: Broadly speaking, the plan was a success.
I broadly agree with what you're saying.
The two studies reached broadly similar conclusions.
He grinned broadly when he saw us.
She was smiling broadly as she accepted the award.

senses.head: In general, without the details
examples: Broadly speaking, the plan was a success.
I broadly agree with what you're saying.
The two studies reached broadly similar conclusions.

senses.head: Widely and openly, of a smile
examples: He grinned broadly when he saw us.
She was smiling broadly as she accepted the award.

entries.position: front — broadly speaking; also mid or end

entries.meaning: In general, ignoring details and exceptions. ---
examples: Broadly speaking, prices in the city are higher.
Broadly speaking, there are two kinds of learners.
The results were, broadly speaking, positive.
entries.form: broadly + speaking, like generally speaking and strictly speaking

entries.meaning: With the whole side facing or hit by something. ---
examples: A truck ran the red light and hit our car broadside.
The boat was struck broadside by a huge wave.
The ship swung broadside to the wind.
entries.modifies: verbs of hitting and turning, mainly hit and strike
entries.contrast: More often a noun: launch a broadside against the mayor means to attack him in strong words. For cars, everyday American speech also says T-boned.

entries.meaning: In a short, rude, abrupt way. ---
examples: "Not now," he said brusquely.
The nurse brusquely told us to wait outside.
She answered brusquely and hung up.

entries.meaning: Brutally has 2 distinct senses.
examples: The prisoners were brutally beaten.
The protest was brutally put down by the army.
To be brutally honest, I didn't like the movie.
It was a brutally hot summer in Phoenix.
The schedule was brutally demanding.

senses.head: In a very cruel or violent way
examples: The prisoners were brutally beaten.
The protest was brutally put down by the army.

senses.head: Extremely, of something harsh or unpleasant
examples: To be brutally honest, I didn't like the movie.
It was a brutally hot summer in Phoenix.
The schedule was brutally demanding.

entries.position: end — before its word as a degree word: brutally honest

entries.meaning: In an active way, with a lot to do. ---
examples: The staff were busily preparing for the holidays.
She was typing busily when I walked in.
Bees buzzed busily around the flowers.

entries.meaning: But has 2 distinct senses.
examples: She was but a child when the war began.
This is but one example of the problem.
Life is but a dream.
By noon the snow had all but disappeared.
Finishing on time is now all but impossible.

senses.head: Only; no more than
examples: She was but a child when the war began.
This is but one example of the problem.
Life is but a dream.

senses.head: Almost, in the phrase all but
examples: By noon the snow had all but disappeared.
Finishing on time is now all but impossible.

entries.type: focusing — formal; also degree in all but
entries.contrast: Normally a conjunction (small but strong). As an adverb meaning only it is formal or literary. All but before an adjective or verb means almost (all but impossible), but before a noun it means everyone or everything except (all but one).

entries.meaning: On the other hand; but it should be remembered that. ---
examples: The food was expensive, but then it was the best in town.
He's not very fit — but then he's almost eighty.
I might go. But then again, I might not.
entries.русский: но ведь, но с другой стороны
entries.type: linking — balances or explains what was said
entries.contrast: Not a time sequence like and then (потом): but then adds a fact that explains or balances the last one. But then again is the same, more tentative.

entries.meaning: By a long shot has 2 distinct senses.
examples: The fight isn't over — not by a long shot.
She isn't the best player on the team by a long shot.
It was the hardest exam of the year by a long shot.
He was the strongest candidate by a long shot.

senses.head: At all, with not; used to make a negative stronger
examples: The fight isn't over — not by a long shot.
She isn't the best player on the team by a long shot.

senses.head: By a large amount, with a superlative; clearly
examples: It was the hardest exam of the year by a long shot.
He was the strongest candidate by a long shot.

entries.русский: далеко не; безусловно, с большим отрывом
entries.type: degree — strengthens a negative or a superlative
entries.modifies: a negative clause or a superlative
entries.contrast: A long shot alone is a noun: an attempt unlikely to succeed. Not by a long shot is informal American for not at all.

entries.meaning: Without intending to. ---
examples: I deleted the file by accident.
We met by accident at the airport.
She found the letter by accident while cleaning.
entries.position: end — after the verb and its object
entries.contrast: The standard preposition is by. On accident is common in the speech of younger Americans but is still considered nonstandard in writing; never ✗ in accident. The opposite is on purpose.

entries.meaning: Certainly; of course, used to give permission or encourage. ---
examples: 'Mind if I sit here?' 'By all means.'
By all means, call me if you need anything.
If you want to try it, by all means go ahead.
entries.position: front — often alone as a reply
entries.contrast: Opposite of by no means (ни в коем случае, вовсе не), though the words look alike.

entries.meaning: On the whole; generally speaking. ---
examples: By and large, the reviews were positive.
The kids behaved well, by and large.
By and large, Americans tip about twenty percent.
entries.русский: в общем и целом, в основном
entries.contrast: The words do not explain it: it has nothing to do with size.

entries.meaning: By any means has 2 distinct senses.
examples: It's not a perfect solution by any means.
She isn't rich by any means.
They were determined to win by any means necessary.
Get the data by any means you can.

senses.head: In any way; at all, with a negative
examples: It's not a perfect solution by any means.
She isn't rich by any means.

senses.head: In whatever way is possible
examples: They were determined to win by any means necessary.
Get the data by any means you can.

entries.modifies: a negative clause; verbs of getting and doing
entries.contrast: Not by any means equals by no means. By any means necessary means doing whatever it takes.

entries.meaning: Without planning; accidentally. ---
examples: We met by chance at the airport.
I found the letter purely by chance.
Do you by chance have a pen?
entries.position: mid or end — mid in polite questions (Do you by chance…?)
entries.contrast: In a polite question it means perhaps: Do you by chance know her? (вы случайно не знаете её?) — Russian случайно works the same way.

entries.meaning: Because one wants to, not because one has to. ---
examples: She lives alone by choice.
Are you working late by choice?
He's a vegetarian by choice, not for health reasons.
entries.modifies: verbs, and be with a noun

entries.meaning: On purpose; as planned. ---
examples: The delay was no accident; it was by design.
The room is small by design, to keep it warm.
Whether by design or by accident, he missed the meeting.
entries.contrast: The opposite of by accident. Design here means intention, not drawing or style.

entries.meaning: By a great amount; clearly. ---
examples: This is by far the best pizza in town.
She was the fastest runner by far.
Walking is by far the cheapest option.
entries.position: before its word — or end (the best by far)
entries.contrast: Mainly with superlatives: by far the best. With a comparative, far better or much better is more natural than better by far.

entries.meaning: By hand has 2 distinct senses.
examples: All the dresses are sewn by hand.
I washed the dishes by hand.
The labels were written by hand.
The invitation was delivered by hand.
Please take these documents to the court by hand.

senses.head: Using the hands, not a machine
examples: All the dresses are sewn by hand.
I washed the dishes by hand.
The labels were written by hand.

senses.head: Delivered in person, not by mail
examples: The invitation was delivered by hand.
Please take these documents to the court by hand.

entries.modifies: verbs of making, writing, washing and delivering
entries.contrast: No article or possessive: by hand, not by my hands.

entries.meaning: From memory. ---
examples: She knows the whole song by heart.
We had to learn the poem by heart.
I know his number by heart.
entries.contrast: Not at heart (в душе).

entries.meaning: By any means possible, fair or unfair. ---
examples: He was going to get that job by hook or by crook.
By hook or by crook, we'll finish on time.
She got tickets to the show by hook or by crook.

entries.meaning: Because of one's basic character. ---
examples: He's a cautious person by nature.
Cats are curious by nature.
I am by nature an optimist.
entries.position: mid or end — mid after be (She is by nature shy)
entries.modifies: be with a noun or adjective

entries.meaning: Not at all; certainly not. ---
examples: The test was by no means easy.
This is by no means the first time it's happened.
By no means is the problem solved.
entries.русский: ни в коем случае, вовсе не
entries.position: mid — after be or the first auxiliary; or front with inversion
entries.contrast: At the front it triggers inversion: By no means is the problem solved. Do not confuse with by all means (конечно).

entries.meaning: If things were fair or correct. ---
examples: By rights, the house should have gone to her.
He should, by rights, be in jail.
By rights we ought to have won that game.
entries.position: any position — front, mid after should, or end
entries.modifies: a clause, usually with should or ought to

entries.meaning: By the day has 2 distinct senses.
examples: You can rent a bike by the day.
The workers are paid by the day.
The situation is getting worse by the day.
The baby is growing by the day.

senses.head: Paid, rented or counted one day at a time
examples: You can rent a bike by the day.
The workers are paid by the day.

senses.head: With each day that passes; steadily
examples: The situation is getting worse by the day.
The baby is growing by the day.

entries.modifies: verbs of paying and renting; verbs of change

entries.meaning: Used to add something unrelated or to change the subject. ---
examples: By the way, your mom called.
What's your name, by the way?
I saw Mike yesterday — he says hi, by the way.
entries.contrast: Written BTW in texts. On the way (по пути) and in the way (мешать) are different phrases.

entries.meaning: By trying different ways and learning from mistakes. ---
examples: I learned to cook mostly by trial and error.
They found the right settings by trial and error.
Many early medicines were discovered by trial and error.

entries.meaning: By people telling each other, not through print or advertising. ---
examples: The restaurant became popular by word of mouth.
News of the layoffs spread by word of mouth.
Most of our customers find us by word of mouth.
entries.modifies: verbs of spreading, learning and finding
entries.contrast: Also an adjective with hyphens: word-of-mouth advertising (сарафанное радио).

entries.meaning: In the Common Era; the same years as A.D., used after a year. ---
examples: Mount Vesuvius erupted in 79 C.E.
The city was founded around 300 C.E.
By the fifth century C.E., the empire had split in two.
entries.position: after its word — after the year or century
entries.form: abbreviation of Common Era; also written CE
entries.contrast: C.E. goes after the year (79 C.E.), while the older A.D. traditionally goes before it (A.D. 79).

entries.meaning: In a careful, secretive way that avoids giving information. ---
examples: He answered cagily when asked about his plans.
The senator spoke cagily about a run for president.
She smiled cagily and changed the subject.

entries.meaning: In a cruel way that shows no concern for others' feelings. ---
examples: The company callously fired workers by text message.
He callously ignored her pleas for help.
The refugees were treated callously at the border.

entries.meaning: In a quiet, relaxed way, without getting upset. ---
examples: She calmly explained what had happened.
Please walk calmly to the nearest exit.
He took the bad news calmly.

entries.meaning: In an honest, open way. ---
examples: She spoke candidly about her divorce.
Candidly, I don't think the plan will work.
He candidly admitted he had made a mistake.
entries.position: end — also front, as a comment

entries.meaning: In a clever, shrewd way, especially about money or business. ---
examples: She cannily bought the property before prices rose.
The campaign cannily targeted young voters.
He had cannily saved for years.

entries.meaning: With skill and competence. ---
examples: She handled the crisis capably.
The deputy ran the office capably while the boss was away.
The team capably managed a very difficult project.

entries.meaning: In a sudden, unpredictable way, without a good reason. ---
examples: The rules seemed to be applied capriciously.
The weather changes capriciously in the mountains.
The manager fired people capriciously.

entries.meaning: Carefully has 2 distinct senses.
examples: Drive carefully — the roads are icy.
She carefully lifted the baby out of the car seat.
Please read the instructions carefully.
The speech had been carefully planned.
Listen carefully to what I'm about to say.

senses.head: With caution, so as to avoid harm or damage
examples: Drive carefully — the roads are icy.
She carefully lifted the baby out of the car seat.

senses.head: With close attention to detail; thoroughly
examples: Please read the instructions carefully.
The speech had been carefully planned.
Listen carefully to what I'm about to say.

entries.meaning: Without enough care or attention. ---
examples: He carelessly left the front door unlocked.
Someone had carelessly tossed a cigarette into the dry grass.
Her coat was thrown carelessly over a chair.

entries.meaning: Casually has 2 distinct senses.
examples: He casually mentioned that he'd quit his job.
She leaned casually against the wall.
He glanced casually at the clock, trying not to look nervous.
Most people at the office dress casually on Fridays.
The guests were casually dressed in jeans and T-shirts.

senses.head: In a relaxed, offhand way, without much thought or attention
examples: He casually mentioned that he'd quit his job.
She leaned casually against the wall.
He glanced casually at the clock, trying not to look nervous.

senses.head: In an informal way, especially about clothes
examples: Most people at the office dress casually on Fridays.
The guests were casually dressed in jeans and T-shirts.

entries.meaning: In a way that causes or amounts to a disaster. ---
examples: The bridge failed catastrophically during the storm.
The plan went catastrophically wrong.
A catastrophically bad harvest left thousands of families hungry.
entries.position: end — also before an adjective (catastrophically bad)

entries.meaning: Absolutely and without any doubt or exception. ---
examples: The senator categorically denied the report.
We categorically reject any form of violence.
I can tell you categorically that no one was hurt.
entries.position: mid — before verbs like deny, reject, refuse; also end
entries.modifies: verbs of saying, denying and refusing

entries.meaning: As cause and effect. ---
examples: The two events are not causally related.
Smoking is causally linked to lung cancer.
The study could not show that the drug and the side effects were causally connected.
entries.position: before its word — usually before related, linked, connected
entries.contrast: Do not confuse with casually (небрежно) — the same letters in a different order. Causally related means one thing causes the other; casually related is a misprint.

entries.meaning: In a bitterly sarcastic, critical way. ---
examples: "Thanks for nothing," she said caustically.
He wrote caustically about the new mayor.
The critic caustically dismissed the movie as a two-hour commercial.

entries.meaning: Carefully, so as to avoid risk or mistakes. ---
examples: She stepped cautiously onto the ice.
Doctors are cautiously optimistic about his recovery.
Drive cautiously — the roads are still wet.

entries.meaning: In an offhand, dismissive way that ignores serious concerns or other people's feelings. ---
examples: The company treated its customers' complaints cavalierly.
He cavalierly brushed aside the safety warnings.
Our personal data was handled rather cavalierly.

entries.meaning: Without stopping, for a long time. ---
examples: The rain fell ceaselessly for three days.
She worked ceaselessly to get her brother released.
The waves beat ceaselessly against the rocks.

entries.meaning: Centrally has 2 distinct senses.
examples: The hotel is centrally located, close to all the museums.
We need an office that is more centrally placed.
The heating in the building is controlled centrally.
The Soviet economy was centrally planned.

senses.head: In or near the center of a place
examples: The hotel is centrally located, close to all the museums.
We need an office that is more centrally placed.

senses.head: From one central place or authority rather than locally
examples: The heating in the building is controlled centrally.
The Soviet economy was centrally planned.

entries.position: before its word — before a participle (centrally located); also end

entries.meaning: As part of a formal ceremony or ritual. ---
examples: The new bridge was ceremonially opened by the governor.
Every evening the flag is ceremonially lowered.
The keys to the city were ceremonially handed to the astronauts.
entries.position: before its word — before a participle; also end

entries.meaning: In a completely disorganized, confused way. ---
examples: Kids ran chaotically around the playground.
The evacuation was handled chaotically.
Papers were piled chaotically on every desk.

entries.meaning: In a way that is typical of a particular person or thing. ---
examples: Characteristically, she arrived early and stayed late.
He was characteristically modest about his success.
The speech was characteristically short and blunt.
entries.position: front — also before an adjective (characteristically modest)
entries.modifies: a whole clause, adjectives, and verbs

entries.meaning: In a kind, generous way that judges others favorably. ---
examples: To put it charitably, the movie was not his best work.
She charitably assumed he had simply forgotten.
Try to view their mistakes a little more charitably.
entries.position: end — also front in to put it charitably
entries.modifies: verbs of judging, describing and treating

entries.meaning: In a pleasant, attractive way. ---
examples: The inn is charmingly old-fashioned.
He smiled charmingly at the waitress.
The story is simple but charmingly told.

She looked critically at her reflection.

senses.head: So seriously that life is in danger
examples: Two people were critically injured in the crash.
He is critically ill.

senses.head: Extremely; at a decisive level
examples: Clean water is critically important after a flood.
Blood supplies are critically low this month.

entries.modifies: verbs; adjectives such as ill, injured, important, low

entries.meaning: At an angle; not straight. ---
examples: The picture hung crookedly on the wall.
He grinned crookedly at me.
Her glasses sat crookedly on her nose.

entries.meaning: Cross-country has 2 distinct senses.
examples: We drove cross-country after graduation.
They flew cross-country to see her parents.
The horses galloped cross-country.
They skied cross-country to the lodge.

senses.head: Across a whole country, especially from one coast to the other
examples: We drove cross-country after graduation.
They flew cross-country to see her parents.

senses.head: Across fields and open land rather than along roads
examples: The horses galloped cross-country.
They skied cross-country to the lodge.

entries.русский: через всю страну; по пересечённой местности
entries.form: compound — also an adjective (a cross-country race)

entries.meaning: With the legs crossed, especially sitting on the floor with the knees apart. ---
examples: The kids sat cross-legged on the rug.
She sat cross-legged on the bed, reading.
He was sitting cross-legged in front of the TV.

entries.meaning: Across a city, from one side to the other. ---
examples: We took a cab crosstown to the theater.
The bus runs crosstown along 42nd Street.
She moved crosstown to be closer to her office.
entries.form: compound — also an adjective (a crosstown bus)

entries.meaning: Across; at a right angle to the length of something. ---
examples: Slice the carrots crosswise into thin rounds.
Lay the boards crosswise over the ditch.
Fold the napkin crosswise.

entries.meaning: Crucially has 2 distinct senses.
examples: Crucially, the test was done before the drug was approved.
The plan is cheap and, crucially, fast.
Timing is crucially important here.
The outcome depends crucially on the weather.

senses.head: Most importantly; used to point out the key fact
examples: Crucially, the test was done before the drug was approved.
The plan is cheap and, crucially, fast.

senses.head: In a decisive way; to a very great degree
examples: Timing is crucially important here.
The outcome depends crucially on the weather.

entries.modifies: a whole clause; adjectives and verbs (crucially important, depends crucially)

entries.meaning: Crudely has 2 distinct senses.
examples: The sign was crudely painted on a board.
The shelter was crudely built from branches.
To put it crudely, they just want your money.
He joked crudely about her looks.
The comedian spoke crudely all night.

senses.head: In a rough, simple way, without skill or detail
examples: The sign was crudely painted on a board.
The shelter was crudely built from branches.
To put it crudely, they just want your money.

senses.head: In a vulgar, offensive way
examples: He joked crudely about her looks.
The comedian spoke crudely all night.

entries.meaning: In a way that causes pain or suffering, on purpose or with painful unfairness. ---
examples: The prisoners were treated cruelly.
He laughed cruelly at her mistake.
Her career was cruelly cut short by injury.

entries.meaning: Overwhelmingly; to a crushing degree. ---
examples: The lecture was crushingly dull.
Rents here are crushingly expensive.
The incumbent was crushingly defeated.

entries.meaning: In a mysterious way that is hard to understand. ---
examples: 'Wait and see,' she said cryptically.
He posted a cryptically worded message.
The note was signed cryptically with a single letter.

entries.meaning: With academic honors, at the end of a degree. ---
examples: She graduated cum laude from Yale.
He finished cum laude in economics.
About a quarter of the class graduated cum laude.
entries.contrast: American honors, from lowest to highest: cum laude, magna cum laude, summa cum laude. Also pronounced /kʌm ˈlɔːdi/.

entries.meaning: Taken together; by adding up over time. ---
examples: Cumulatively, these small cuts save millions.
The effects of lost sleep build up cumulatively.
Small changes can cumulatively make a big difference.

entries.meaning: Cunningly has 2 distinct senses.
examples: He cunningly hid the losses from investors.
She cunningly played the two rivals against each other.
The drawer is cunningly hidden in the desk.
The tiny apartment is cunningly designed.

senses.head: In a sly, deceptive way
examples: He cunningly hid the losses from investors.
She cunningly played the two rivals against each other.

senses.head: Cleverly and skillfully
examples: The drawer is cunningly hidden in the desk.
The tiny apartment is cunningly designed.

entries.meaning: Quickly and without attention to detail. ---
examples: He glanced cursorily at the contract and signed it.
The report was only cursorily reviewed.
The inspector looked cursorily around the kitchen.

entries.meaning: In a rudely short way. ---
examples: 'No,' she said curtly.
He nodded curtly and left.
The email curtly informed him that his contract was over.

entries.meaning: As is usual or traditional. ---
examples: The bride's family customarily pays for the wedding.
Tips are customarily about twenty percent.
The award is customarily presented in the spring.

entries.meaning: In a way that assumes the worst about people's motives, or that exploits others without caring.
examples: Some voters cynically assume all politicians lie.
He smiled cynically when she mentioned loyalty.
The ad cynically exploits people's fears.
